questions.title: Fine-Tuning vs. Prompting vs. LoRA: Choosing the Right Lever
questions.prompt: Your team is building an internal support assistant that must consistently adopt a specific tone, cite internal policy codes in an exact format, and never use a list of banned phrases. Someone proposes solving it with better prompting, someone else wants to run full fine-tuning on a few thousand examples, and a third person suggests LoRA. Explain the real mechanical difference between prompting and fine-tuning -- what each one actually changes inside the system -- and then explain how you would decide between prompting, LoRA, and full fine-tuning for this specific case.
questions.modelAnswer:
Prompting and fine-tuning change two completely different things, even though both can alter a model's observed behavior. Prompting changes the input: it adds instructions, examples, or context into the sequence the model conditions on at inference time. The model's weights never move; every apparent 'learning' from a few-shot example is the model using its frozen attention and feed-forward computations to recognize a pattern in the current context window and extrapolate from it. That means the behavior is scoped to that single request, consumes context tokens, has to be re-specified every time, and is bounded by how reliably the model can generalize a pattern from a handful of examples under everything else competing for its attention in that prompt.

Fine-tuning changes the weights themselves through gradient descent on a labeled dataset, so the desired behavior becomes part of the model's learned parameters rather than something re-supplied at inference time. Full fine-tuning updates every parameter, which requires the most compute and memory, carries the highest risk of catastrophic forgetting of unrelated capabilities, and is usually only justified when the task requires deep, broad behavioral change. LoRA instead freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices inserted into specific layers -- typically well under 1% of the total parameter count -- then applies those adapters at inference time. It captures most of the benefit of fine-tuning for narrower, pattern-level behaviors at a small fraction of the cost and with far less risk of degrading the base model's general skills.

For this scenario, tone, a fixed citation format, and a banned-phrase list are exactly the kind of persistent, pattern-level behavior that prompting alone tends to enforce unreliably once volume and input variety scale up -- formatting drifts, banned phrases slip back in on edge cases, and the system prompt has to grow to cover every exception. That rules out pure prompting as the sole long-term solution but doesn't require the depth of change that would justify full fine-tuning's cost and forgetting risk. LoRA is the right lever: a few hundred to a few thousand well-labeled examples are usually enough to bake the format and tone in reliably, iteration is cheap enough to retrain when policy codes change, and the base model's general reasoning stays intact. The practical path is to prototype with prompting first to see exactly where it breaks down, then move to LoRA once that gap is clear.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by making sure the interviewer and I agree on what each technique is actually touching, because people conflate them constantly. Prompting never touches the model -- it's purely an input-side trick. Every time you give a few-shot example or a style instruction, you're relying on the model's frozen weights to do in-context pattern matching on the fly, which is powerful but temporary and token-hungry: you're paying for it on every single call and it competes with everything else you're trying to stuff into the context window. Fine-tuning is the opposite: you're literally changing the numbers inside the model through training, so the behavior sticks around without being re-explained every time.

Then I'd walk through the LoRA piece specifically, because that's usually where the real decision lives in practice -- nobody reaches for full fine-tuning lightly anymore. I'd explain LoRA as training a small set of adapter matrices that sit alongside the frozen original weights rather than touching them directly, so you get most of the behavioral change you want for a fraction of the GPU cost and without the risk of wrecking the model's general abilities, which is a real risk with full fine-tuning on a narrow dataset.

For the actual scenario -- tone, a fixed citation format, banned phrases -- I'd say out loud that this is a textbook LoRA case, not a full fine-tune, and definitely not something I'd trust pure prompting to hold up under production volume. Tone and format are consistent, narrow patterns, which is exactly what a small adapter is good at learning from a modest labeled set; full fine-tuning would be overkill and riskier for forgetting, and prompting alone tends to degrade as soon as inputs get varied enough that your system prompt can't anticipate every edge case. I'd probably mention that I'd still start with a prompting prototype, not because it's the final answer, but because it's the cheapest way to find out exactly which behaviors prompting can't hold reliably -- that gap is your LoRA training set.
questions.example: Rough signal for the decision: prompting handles 'answer in a friendly tone' fine; LoRA is needed when you see format drift like citing a policy code as 'Policy 4' instead of 'POL-004' in roughly one out of twenty generations despite the system prompt explicitly specifying the format every time.
commonMistakes: Treating fine-tuning as a universal upgrade over prompting instead of a different mechanism with its own tradeoffs
Assuming LoRA and full fine-tuning differ only in cost, without explaining that LoRA trains a small adapter while the base weights stay frozen
Reaching for full fine-tuning for a narrow stylistic task that LoRA or even strong prompting could solve more cheaply
Ignoring catastrophic forgetting as a real risk of full fine-tuning on a small, narrow dataset
Failing to mention that prompting has no training cost but pays a recurring token cost on every request
keyPoints: Prompting conditions the frozen model via in-context learning; it changes the input, not the weights
Fine-tuning updates weights via gradient descent so behavior persists without being re-specified
LoRA trains small low-rank adapter matrices while freezing the base model, cutting cost and forgetting risk
Full fine-tuning updates all parameters and is only justified for deep, broad behavioral change
The decision should map task scope (narrow/stylistic vs. deep/broad) to the matching technique, prototyping with prompting first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains prompting as input-side, no weight change
Correctly explains fine-tuning as weight updates via gradient descent
Accurately describes LoRA's low-rank adapter mechanism and cost benefit
Gives a well-reasoned recommendation for the specific scenario
Mentions forgetting risk / cost tradeoffs appropriately

questions.title: How LoRA Actually Reduces the Cost of Fine-Tuning
questions.prompt: A teammate without a deep ML background asks why your startup can fine-tune a 7-billion-parameter model on a single GPU when they thought that required a data center. Explain mechanically how LoRA works -- what the low-rank adapter matrices are doing and where they sit relative to the frozen base weights -- and then explain specifically why this changes the cost and feasibility calculus for a team without a large GPU budget.
questions.modelAnswer:
Full fine-tuning is expensive primarily because of what it drags along with the weights, not the weights themselves. Training requires storing gradients for every parameter plus optimizer state (for example, Adam keeps roughly two extra value per parameter beyond the weight itself), on top of activation memory needed for backpropagation. For a 7-billion-parameter model, that adds up to tens of gigabytes of memory beyond the base weights, which is exactly why full fine-tuning typically requires multiple high-memory GPUs working together.

LoRA sidesteps most of that cost by freezing the original weight matrix W entirely and instead learning a low-rank update represented as two small matrices, commonly called A and B, inserted alongside specific layers -- most often the attention projection matrices. The effective weight during inference becomes the frozen W plus the product of B and A, where both matrices share a small rank r (often somewhere between 8 and 64) that is far smaller than W's own dimensions. Critically, gradients and optimizer state only need to be computed and stored for A and B, not for W, which shrinks the trainable parameter count to typically well under 1% of the full model.

That reduction in trainable parameters directly translates to a reduction in GPU memory required for training, since the dominant memory cost during fine-tuning is gradients and optimizer state, not the frozen weights sitting in memory for the forward pass. This is what lets a 7-billion-parameter model be adapted on a single GPU instead of a cluster, shortens iteration cycles since retraining is cheap, and lets a team store and swap many small task-specific adapters against one shared frozen base model instead of duplicating the entire model per task, since each adapter is only megabytes rather than gigabytes.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain it with the cost breakdown first, because that's what actually lands for someone non-technical. Full fine-tuning isn't expensive because of the model weights themselves, it's expensive because of everything training drags along with them -- gradients and optimizer state for every single parameter, which for a 7-billion-parameter model is a genuinely large amount of extra memory on top of the model itself. That's the real reason it needs serious hardware.

Then I'd use a sticky-note analogy for LoRA: instead of rewriting the whole book, which is what full fine-tuning does, you attach small sticky notes with corrections at specific pages. The book itself -- the frozen weight matrix -- never gets rewritten; you only ever need to store and update the sticky notes, which are the small low-rank A and B matrices. Because those sticky notes are tiny compared to the book, the gradients and optimizer state you need to track during training shrink by the same proportion, which is the entire reason the memory footprint collapses.

The practical payoff I'd emphasize is what that unlocks for a small team: you can fine-tune on a single GPU instead of a cluster, you can afford to retrain quickly when requirements change, and you can keep a handful of small task-specific adapters around for one shared base model instead of paying to store and serve a full duplicate model per use case. That last point matters more than people expect -- it turns fine-tuning from a rare, expensive event into something you can iterate on like any other part of the product.
questions.example: Concretely: a 7-billion-parameter model's attention projection matrix might be 4096x4096 (about 16.7 million parameters); a LoRA adapter with rank 8 replaces the trainable portion with a 4096x8 matrix and an 8x4096 matrix -- about 65,000 trainable parameters for that layer instead of 16.7 million.
commonMistakes: Describing LoRA as 'a smaller version of the model' rather than a frozen base plus trainable adapters
Forgetting that optimizer state and gradient memory, not just weight storage, are what make full fine-tuning expensive
Assuming LoRA always matches full fine-tuning quality regardless of task complexity
Not mentioning that multiple LoRA adapters can be swapped on one frozen base model for different tasks
Confusing LoRA's rank hyperparameter with the number of layers it is applied to
keyPoints: Full fine-tuning cost comes primarily from gradients and optimizer state across all parameters, not just weight storage
LoRA freezes the base weight matrix W and learns a low-rank update via two small matrices A and B
Only the small adapter matrices need gradients and optimizer state, cutting memory requirements drastically
Rank r controls the adapter's capacity and is far smaller than the original matrix dimensions
Lower memory and storage enable single-GPU fine-tuning and cheap multi-task adapter swapping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why full fine-tuning is memory-expensive (gradients/optimizer state)
Correctly describes the frozen W plus low-rank BA mechanism
Explains the resulting reduction in trainable parameters and memory
Connects this to practical cost/feasibility outcomes for small teams
Clear, accurate, appropriately pitched explanation

questions.title: How Vision-Language Models Fuse Image and Text Tokens
questions.prompt: Your team is integrating a vision-language model so support agents can upload a screenshot alongside a text question. During testing, a teammate notices that uploading a high-resolution screenshot causes the model to effectively forget instructions given earlier in a long system prompt. Explain mechanically what happens inside a vision-language model when it processes an image alongside text -- how the image ends up represented alongside text tokens -- and explain why this specific failure happens.
questions.modelAnswer:
A vision-language model processes an image through a vision encoder, often a vision transformer in the style of CLIP, which converts the image into a grid of patch embeddings -- numeric vectors, one per small region of the image. A projection layer then maps those patch embeddings into the same dimensional space the language model uses for its own text token embeddings. Those projected patches become image tokens that get inserted directly into the input sequence alongside the ordinary text tokens, so by the time the transformer's self-attention layers run, image tokens and text tokens are simply vectors living in one shared representation space, attending to each other exactly as text tokens attend to other text tokens.

There is no separate vision pathway operating at inference time; it is a single combined sequence. The model does not 'see' an image the way a human does -- it processes a set of embedding vectors derived from pixels through the vision encoder, and relies entirely on attention across the combined sequence to relate those vectors to the text tokens asking about them.

The forgetting happens because a high-resolution image can be split into hundreds of patches, each becoming its own token, so a single screenshot can consume many hundreds to low thousands of tokens of the model's context window budget. If the system prompt sits early in the sequence and the image tokens plus the user's question push the total length close to or past the context limit, earlier instructions can be truncated outright, or even where they technically remain in-window, they get diluted -- competing for attention weight against a large block of image tokens, compounded by the well-documented tendency for content positioned away from the current turn to receive weaker effective attention in long sequences. The fix is to budget image token cost explicitly like any other context item, place critical instructions where they are reliably attended to, and resize or compress images to the resolution actually needed rather than defaulting to maximum resolution.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell them: once the image hits the vision encoder, it stops being a picture at all from the model's perspective. It becomes a sequence of numeric vectors -- one per image patch, like tiles on a grid -- that get reshaped through a small projection step until they're the exact same shape as a word embedding. After that, the model literally cannot tell whether a given position in its input sequence came from a pixel patch or from a word; it's just attention running over one combined sequence.

The part I'd flag as the real culprit here is that every image is implicitly a token-count surprise. A single high-resolution screenshot can turn into the rough token equivalent of a one- or two-page document, and that eats into exactly the same shared budget as your system prompt, your conversation history, everything. So when the teammate says the model 'forgot' the earlier instructions, I'd reframe that as a budget problem, not a comprehension problem -- either the instructions got pushed out of the window entirely once the image tokens were added, or they're technically still there but buried far enough from the current turn that they get weaker attention, the same 'lost in the middle' effect you see with any very long text-only prompt.

My fix would be practical: treat image token cost as a first-class line item when budgeting context, resize images down to the resolution the task actually needs instead of uploading at maximum resolution by default, and if certain instructions absolutely cannot be allowed to drift out of effective attention, consider repeating the critical ones closer to the end of the prompt, right before the model has to act on them.
questions.example: A single 1024x1024 screenshot run through a typical patch-based vision encoder can easily produce 500 to 1,500 image tokens -- the rough equivalent of a one- to two-page document -- silently eating into the same budget as the system prompt and conversation history.
commonMistakes: Describing images as processed through a separate pathway that stays distinct from the text context
Not realizing image patches become discrete tokens that consume the same context window budget as text
Assuming higher image resolution is always better without considering the token cost
Attributing the instruction-forgetting purely to the model being confused by images rather than context budget and position effects
Failing to mention mitigation strategies like image resizing or instruction placement
keyPoints: A vision encoder converts the image into patch embeddings, projected into the language model's embedding space
Image tokens and text tokens are concatenated into one sequence attended to jointly by the transformer
Image tokens consume real context window budget, often hundreds to thousands of tokens per image
Long sequences suffer position-dependent attention degradation, which compounds the truncation risk
Practical mitigation includes resizing images, budgeting token cost, and positioning critical instructions carefully

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the vision encoder producing patch embeddings
Explains projection into a shared embedding space with text tokens
Explains that image and text tokens are attended to jointly, not through separate pathways
Correctly diagnoses the forgetting as a context budget / token cost issue
Offers a credible practical mitigation

questions.title: Why LLMs Hallucinate Is Not a Data Problem
questions.prompt: After a factual error slips into production, a product manager asks why you can't just train the model on more correct data to fix hallucinations for good. Explain, at a mechanistic level, why LLMs hallucinate -- rooted in how next-token prediction training actually works -- and explain why this means hallucination isn't simply a bug that more or better training data eliminates.
questions.modelAnswer:
LLMs are trained to predict the most statistically plausible next token given preceding context, optimizing a loss function over massive text corpora. That objective rewards fluent, plausible continuations, not verified, grounded truth. The model has no built-in mechanism that distinguishes confidently recalling a fact from producing the most probable-sounding sequence of words, because both pass through exactly the same computation: next-token probability estimation conditioned on everything that came before.

Critically, when the model has little or no strong signal for the next token in the training distribution -- an obscure fact, something poorly represented -- it does not default to admitting uncertainty, because that behavior has to be explicitly shaped through techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback or targeted instruction tuning. The pretraining objective alone just produces the next most probable token, which under uncertainty tends to be a plausible-sounding but possibly fabricated continuation rather than an acknowledgment of ignorance. Hallucination is therefore an inherent consequence of generating from a learned probability distribution shaped mostly by plausibility, not a separate defect in the implementation.

More data does not eliminate this because the mechanism producing hallucination is the same mechanism producing the model's real capability: generating from a learned distribution and extrapolating under uncertainty. More data narrows that distribution and improves calibration for well-covered facts, but it cannot give the model certainty about facts it has sparse or conflicting coverage of, and it does nothing to add a missing truth-verification step at generation time. That is why practical mitigations target the structure around the model rather than the training objective itself -- retrieval augmentation to ground answers in a verifiable source, explicit uncertainty or refusal training, structured output constraints, and downstream fact-checking or citation requirements.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I always explain hallucination with an improv-actor analogy because it defuses the 'just fix the bug' framing immediately. The model was trained to always keep talking in a plausible way, like an improv actor who never breaks character and never says they don't know the scene -- it just keeps generating the next line that sounds right given everything said so far. That's not a glitch, that's literally the training objective: predict the next most probable token. So when it hits a gap in what it actually knows, it doesn't stop, it fills the gap with something fluent and statistically plausible, which is exactly what hallucination is.

I'd push back gently on 'more data fixes it' by pointing out that more data makes the model better at the same game -- predicting plausible text -- it doesn't give the model a conscience or a built-in fact-checker. Even a model trained on an excellent dataset will still hallucinate on questions that fall slightly outside what's well represented, because the architecture has no internal verification step; it's generating from a distribution, not looking anything up.

What I'd actually recommend instead is what we do in practice: retrieval-augmented generation to ground answers against a real, checkable source, explicit training or prompting that rewards the model for saying it doesn't know, and guardrails like requiring citations or running a separate fact-checking pass on high-stakes outputs. I'd frame all of that as working around the root cause, because the root cause -- a model that generates plausible text -- isn't something you train away without changing what the model fundamentally is.
commonMistakes: Calling hallucination a bug or defect rather than a structural consequence of the training objective
Claiming more or cleaner training data will eliminate hallucination entirely
Confusing hallucination with simple factual errors from outdated training data, which is a knowledge-cutoff issue rather than the same mechanism
Assuming the model knows it's uncertain and chooses to lie, rather than lacking a built-in truth-verification step
Failing to mention real mitigations like retrieval augmentation or calibration/refusal training as the actual practical fix
keyPoints: Next-token prediction optimizes for plausible continuations, not verified truth
The model has no built-in mechanism to distinguish confident recall from fluent extrapolation
Under uncertainty, the model defaults to generating plausible text rather than admitting ignorance unless explicitly trained to
More training data improves calibration on well-covered facts but cannot add a missing truth-verification step
Practical mitigations work around the model, such as retrieval augmentation and refusal training, rather than eliminating the root cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains next-token prediction as optimizing plausibility, not truth
Explains why the model fabricates under uncertainty rather than admitting it
Explains clearly why more data doesn't solve the root cause
Mentions credible practical mitigations such as retrieval augmentation or calibration
Clarity and precision of overall explanation

questions.title: When Chain-of-Thought Prompting Helps and When It Backfires
questions.prompt: Your team adds an instruction to think step by step to every prompt in a production pipeline, including a simple sentiment classification endpoint, hoping it improves accuracy everywhere. Latency doubles, costs climb, and accuracy on the sentiment task actually drops slightly. Explain the mechanics of why chain-of-thought prompting measurably improves accuracy on certain tasks, and explain why it failed here instead of helping.
questions.modelAnswer:
Chain-of-thought prompting works by inducing the model to generate intermediate reasoning tokens before committing to a final answer. Because the model is autoregressive, each new token is generated conditioned on all tokens generated so far, including the reasoning tokens it just produced. On tasks that decompose into multiple dependent sub-steps, such as arithmetic, multi-hop inference, or logic puzzles, forcing the model to externalize intermediate steps gives it additional computation and additional conditioning context to build up to a correct final answer, effectively trading inference compute for improved accuracy on tasks whose correct answer genuinely depends on a correct chain of intermediate inferences.

This only helps when the task actually has decomposable, dependent sub-steps where an error can be caught or avoided by reasoning explicitly, and where the model has the latent capability to do each sub-step but struggles to leap straight to the composed answer. Chain-of-thought does not help on tasks that are closer to single-step pattern recognition, because the correct label doesn't depend on deriving intermediate facts, it depends on recognizing a direct mapping from input features to output class.

For sentiment classification, forcing elaborate reasoning can actively hurt: the model may overthink a straightforward sentiment signal, talk itself into an edge case, or latch onto an irrelevant detail it surfaced during the reasoning trace, with each extra generated token also being an opportunity to drift off a correct early impression. The added reasoning tokens also directly explain the latency and cost regression, since chain-of-thought necessarily generates far more output tokens per call. The fix is to apply it selectively, where task structure genuinely benefits from decomposition, and use direct-answer prompting for straightforward classification tasks.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This is one of those 'more reasoning always helps' assumptions that falls apart with a quick mental model of what chain-of-thought is actually doing under the hood. All it's doing is giving the model permission to write out intermediate steps before the final answer, and because it's autoregressive, those written-out steps become extra context it conditions on for the rest of the generation. That's genuinely useful when the task is made of dependent sub-steps -- math, multi-hop logic -- because the model essentially gets to show its work and catch itself partway through.

But sentiment classification isn't that kind of task -- there's no chain of intermediate facts to derive, it's closer to a single-step pattern match. When you force a reasoning trace onto that, you're not giving the model anything useful to condition on, you're giving it rope to talk itself out of an answer it would have gotten right immediately, plus you're paying for every one of those extra tokens in latency and cost. I've genuinely seen chain-of-thought flip a model from correctly flagging mild sarcasm as negative to reasoning its way into thinking the positive-sounding words meant the message was actually positive.

So my fix would be to stop applying it as a blanket default and instead treat it as a per-task decision validated with an actual eval set: keep it for the steps in the pipeline that genuinely involve multi-step reasoning, and strip it entirely from anything closer to direct classification, where a short, direct-answer prompt will be faster, cheaper, and probably more accurate.
questions.example: Rule of thumb I use: if you can't describe the task as a sequence of dependent sub-questions, chain-of-thought is probably adding noise, not signal -- a one-line sentiment label is a one-step task, a word problem is a five-step task.
commonMistakes: Assuming chain-of-thought prompting universally improves accuracy regardless of task type
Not connecting chain-of-thought's benefit to the autoregressive conditioning on self-generated reasoning tokens
Ignoring the latency and cost impact of generating substantially more output tokens
Applying chain-of-thought uniformly across an entire pipeline instead of per task type based on evaluation
Failing to recognize that elaborate reasoning can introduce new errors on straightforward classification tasks
keyPoints: Chain-of-thought works by having the model condition on self-generated intermediate reasoning tokens before the final answer
It helps tasks with decomposable, dependent sub-steps where composing directly is harder than reasoning through steps
It doesn't help, and can hurt, tasks closer to single-step pattern recognition like simple classification
Extra reasoning tokens directly increase latency and cost, which must be weighed against any accuracy gain
Chain-of-thought should be applied selectively per task type and validated with evaluation, not applied as a blanket default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains chain-of-thought's mechanism via autoregressive conditioning on generated reasoning
Correctly identifies the task property that determines chain-of-thought's benefit
Explains why sentiment classification doesn't benefit and can regress
Connects to the observed latency/cost increase
Gives a practical recommendation for selective application

questions.title: Context Window Budgeting Across System Prompt, History, and Tools
questions.prompt: Your agent's context window keeps filling up in long customer conversations: it includes a large system prompt, full conversation history, retrieved documents, and several tool definitions. Users start reporting that the assistant forgets things they said earlier and occasionally ignores instructions that were working fine last week. Explain what it really means to manage a context window budget at scale across these competing consumers, and explain the real failure mode happening here.
questions.modelAnswer:
A context window is a fixed total token budget shared by every component injected into a single request: the system prompt, tool or function definitions, retrieved documents, conversation history, and the current user turn. Managing it at scale means treating that budget as a finite, competing resource explicitly, rather than assuming it will fit -- allocating token ceilings per component, measuring actual token counts rather than characters or rough estimates, and having a deterministic policy for what gets trimmed, summarized, or dropped when the sum exceeds the limit.

Tool definitions add up fast, since each function schema with descriptions and parameters can be hundreds of tokens, and several tools together can be thousands. Full conversation history grows unbounded over a long session, and retrieved documents can be large chunks inserted wholesale. When no one is budgeting across all of these, the overall request can exceed the model's context limit; very commonly, history gets silently truncated from the oldest turns first, or upstream wrapper code sends only part of the conversation. Even short of a hard limit, the system prompt can get crowded out of effective attention long before it's technically removed, because transformers don't attend uniformly across long contexts -- content distant from the current turn tends to receive less effective weight, a well-documented degradation in long-context attention.

The fix is intentional allocation: measure actual tokens per component, assign each a budget where the system prompt and tool definitions are protected fixed overhead, conversation history gets summarized or windowed once it crosses a threshold, and retrieved context gets capped and re-ranked rather than inserted wholesale. Monitoring total tokens per request over time is what catches this kind of regression before users do.
questions.professionalAnswer:
When people say 'manage the context window,' what I actually mean day to day is that I treat every piece of context as a line item competing for a shared, fixed budget, and I literally count tokens for each one -- system prompt, tool schemas, retrieved documents, chat history -- the same way you'd track a budget across departments, not just hope it adds up under the ceiling.

What's happening in this scenario is almost certainly silent overflow. As the conversation grows, nobody capped the history, so eventually the total request -- system prompt plus tools plus history plus retrieval -- blows past the model's limit, and something upstream is quietly cutting it, usually the oldest turns of history first. But even before you hit the hard limit, long contexts suffer attention degradation -- content buried in the middle of a huge prompt just doesn't get weighted as strongly as content near the end, so a system prompt that worked fine last week can start getting effectively ignored purely because the conversation grew and everything around it shifted.

My fix is always the same: measure real token counts per component in production, give each one an explicit ceiling, and have an actual policy -- summarize old history, cap and re-rank retrieved chunks, protect the system prompt's token budget -- instead of leaving it to whatever the API does by default when things overflow.
questions.example: Concretely: reserve about 800 tokens for the system prompt, 1,500 for tool schemas, cap retrieved context at 2,000 tokens after re-ranking, and summarize conversation history into a running digest once raw history exceeds 3,000 tokens, rather than letting all four grow unchecked until something breaks.
commonMistakes: Assuming the API will handle context overflow gracefully without a defined trimming policy
Not accounting for tool and function definitions as a real, sometimes large, token cost
Measuring context size by character count or rough estimate instead of actual tokenization
Letting conversation history grow unbounded instead of summarizing or windowing it
Not recognizing that content far from the current turn gets weaker attention even before hard truncation occurs
keyPoints: The context window is one shared, finite token budget across system prompt, tools, retrieval, and history
Each component should have an explicit token ceiling measured by actual tokenization, not estimated
Tool/function schemas and growing conversation history are common underestimated consumers of the budget
Overflow causes silent truncation, often oldest history first, and can happen before hitting the hard limit because attention degrades over long distances
A deterministic policy such as summarization, re-ranking, and capping must replace relying on default API overflow behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the context window as a shared finite budget across components
Identifies tool definitions and growing history as significant, often underestimated token consumers
Correctly diagnoses silent truncation and attention degradation as the failure mode
Proposes a concrete budgeting/trimming policy
Mentions monitoring/measurement as a preventive practice

questions.title: Why Vector Search Is Approximate, Not Exact, at Scale
questions.prompt: A junior engineer is confused why your RAG system's vector database returns slightly different top-5 results between two nearly identical queries, and asks why you don't just compute exact similarity against every vector to guarantee correctness. Explain what actually happens mechanically at query time in a vector similarity search, and explain why approximate nearest neighbor search is an acceptable, and in fact necessary, tradeoff at scale.
questions.modelAnswer:
At query time, the incoming query text is first converted into an embedding vector by the same or a compatible embedding model used to index the corpus. That query vector is then compared against the stored document vectors using a similarity metric, commonly cosine similarity or dot product, with the goal of finding the k vectors closest to the query vector in that embedding space. An exact nearest-neighbor search would mean computing that similarity against every single stored vector and sorting the results, a linear scan whose cost grows directly with corpus size and dimensionality.

At meaningful production scale, with millions to billions of vectors each having hundreds to low thousands of dimensions, an exact linear scan per query becomes computationally and economically infeasible for interactive latency budgets. Approximate nearest neighbor algorithms, such as HNSW graphs, IVF with clustering, or quantization-based methods, trade a small amount of recall accuracy -- occasionally missing the true single best match, or returning the sixth-closest instead of the fifth -- for large reductions in query latency and compute cost, typically by organizing vectors into a navigable structure that lets the search skip large portions of the space unlikely to contain close matches, rather than visiting every vector.

This is an acceptable tradeoff because RAG's downstream objective tolerates a small amount of recall slop: the difference between retrieving the single best-matching chunk and the second-best-matching chunk is rarely the difference between a correct and incorrect final answer, especially once re-ranking or the LLM's own synthesis smooths over minor ordering differences. The slight nondeterminism between near-identical queries is a direct, expected consequence of approximate graph or cluster traversal depending on exactly where the query vector lands relative to the index structure, and is a reasonable price for keeping retrieval latency low and infrastructure cost bounded as the corpus scales.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by walking through what exact search would actually cost: at query time your text gets embedded into a vector, and to find the truly closest matches you'd need to compare that vector against literally every vector in the index and sort the results. For a toy dataset that's trivial. For millions of documents, that's a full linear scan on every single query, and at that scale it just isn't fast or cheap enough to serve interactively.

I'd explain approximate search with a navigation analogy: it's like asking for directions from someone who knows the neighborhood well instead of checking every single house. Approximate indexes build a kind of shortcut map through the vector space so a query only has to check a small, promising neighborhood instead of everything, and that's exactly why two very similar queries can land in slightly different neighborhoods of that shortcut map and come back with slightly different top-5s.

The thing I'd emphasize is that this is a deliberate, well-understood tradeoff, not a flaw. In a RAG pipeline, missing the literal single best chunk out of thousands of near-duplicates almost never changes whether the final answer is right, especially once you add a re-ranking step on top. I'd rather have fast, slightly imperfect retrieval at scale than exact retrieval that can't keep up with real traffic.
questions.example: On a 50-million-vector index, an exact scan might cost hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per query depending on hardware; an approximate index typically answers the same query in single-digit milliseconds by only visiting a tiny fraction of the index.

questions.title: HNSW Indexing: Recall, Speed, and Memory Tradeoffs
questions.prompt: You're choosing an index type for a vector database holding 200 million embeddings that need sub-50ms retrieval latency. A colleague suggests HNSW by default because that's the standard everyone uses. Explain conceptually how HNSW works well enough to justify its recall, speed, and memory tradeoffs against a flat exact index, and describe a scenario where you would not reach for HNSW.
questions.modelAnswer:
HNSW, short for Hierarchical Navigable Small World, builds a multi-layer graph over the vector set. The top layer contains a sparse subset of vectors connected with long-range links, enabling fast coarse navigation across the space; each successive lower layer contains progressively more vectors with shorter-range, denser links, down to the bottom layer that contains every vector. A query traverses the graph greedily starting at the top layer, moving to whichever connected node is closer to the query vector, and drops down a layer once no closer neighbor is found at the current layer, repeating until it reaches the bottom layer and returns the closest candidates found -- a coarse-to-fine greedy search through a navigable map rather than a scan of everything.

This structure gives HNSW far better than linear query scaling with dataset size in practice, which is why it beats a flat exact index badly on latency at scale, since a flat index guarantees perfect recall but requires a full comparison per query, so latency grows directly with vector count. The tradeoff is recall, since the greedy traversal can occasionally miss a true nearest neighbor trapped in a part of the graph it doesn't explore, though a search-time exhaustiveness parameter lets you trade recall against latency, and memory, since the graph structure itself, storing multiple layers of links per vector, carries meaningfully higher overhead per vector than a flat index that just stores raw vectors, which matters a great deal at hundreds of millions of vectors.

For 200 million vectors needing sub-50ms latency, HNSW's tradeoff is usually worth it and is a reasonable default. The scenario where you would not reach for HNSW includes when the dataset is small enough that a flat index is already fast enough, since the overhead of building and maintaining a graph buys nothing if a brute-force scan already returns in a few milliseconds; when memory is the binding constraint on a very large corpus, favoring an IVF index with quantization instead, which trades more recall and latency for a dramatically smaller memory footprint; or when the index needs to support very frequent inserts and deletes, since HNSW graphs are comparatively costly to update incrementally compared to some cluster-based structures.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd push back gently on 'because everyone uses it' and actually explain the mechanism, because the tradeoff only makes sense once you see what the graph is doing. Picture HNSW as a layered map: the top layer is like a highway system with just a few landmark cities connected by long jumps, so a query can hop across huge distances in the vector space quickly; as you drop down layers the map gets denser, more like local streets, until the bottom layer has every single point. A search zooms in top-down, doing coarse long jumps first and only getting granular near the end, which is why it's so much faster than checking every point directly.

The price you pay is twofold: it's not guaranteed to find the literal true nearest neighbor every time, because the greedy walk through the graph can get stuck in a locally good but not globally best spot, though you can dial that back with the search-time exhaustiveness setting, and the graph itself takes real memory, storing all those layered links per vector, which adds up fast at hundreds of millions of vectors.

I specifically wouldn't default to HNSW if memory is my binding constraint on a huge corpus -- I'd look at an IVF index with product quantization instead, which compresses vectors and accepts more recall loss in exchange for a much smaller footprint. And I wouldn't bother with HNSW at all on a small enough dataset where a flat index is already comfortably fast -- building and tuning a graph for no latency benefit is just extra operational complexity.
questions.example: Rule of thumb: once a flat index's brute-force scan already lands under your latency target, HNSW's added complexity isn't buying you anything.

questions.title: Why Retrieval Pipelines Need a Separate Re-Ranking Stage
questions.prompt: Your RAG system retrieves the top 20 chunks by vector similarity and feeds all of them directly into the LLM's context. Answer quality is inconsistent -- sometimes the most relevant chunk is buried near the bottom of those 20 or crowded out by several mediocre matches. A colleague suggests adding a re-ranking step before context assembly. Explain the mechanics and purpose of re-ranking in a retrieval pipeline, and why a cheap first-pass retrieval often needs a second, more expensive re-ranking stage before the LLM ever sees the context.
questions.modelAnswer:
The initial vector similarity retrieval step, a bi-encoder approach, works by independently embedding the query and each document chunk into vectors ahead of time, or at query time for the query, then comparing them with a cheap distance metric like cosine similarity. This is fast and scalable precisely because the query and document embeddings are computed independently and compared with simple math, which is what makes it feasible to search millions of chunks quickly. That independence is also its core limitation: the embeddings were produced without ever letting the query and a specific document directly interact, so subtle relevance signals that depend on the actual combination of query and document, such as shared specific entities, negation, or precise phrasing overlap, can get lost in the compressed, query-agnostic embedding space.

A re-ranker, typically a cross-encoder, addresses exactly that gap: it takes the query and a candidate document together as a single joint input and runs them through a transformer that lets every token of the query attend directly to every token of the document, producing a much more precise relevance score for that specific pair. This is far more computationally expensive per comparison than a vector dot product, which is exactly why it isn't used for the first-pass search over the entire corpus -- it's applied only to the much smaller candidate set, such as the top 20 to 100, that the cheap first pass already narrowed down, combining the bi-encoder's scalability with the cross-encoder's precision.

In this scenario specifically, re-ranking fixes the described problem because it re-scores and re-orders the same 20 candidates based on a joint, higher-fidelity relevance judgment rather than the embedding-space approximation, reliably pushing the truly most relevant chunk toward the top and letting you discard the mediocre ones rather than feeding all 20 indiscriminately into the LLM's limited and position-sensitive context window, which matters because content buried in the middle of a large context block tends to get less effective attention weight from the LLM regardless of how relevant it actually is.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain it as a two-round-dating analogy. The first retrieval pass, vector similarity, is like speed dating: the query and documents were never actually in the same room together, they were each summarized into a profile ahead of time and you're just comparing profiles mathematically. That's fast enough to do across millions of candidates, but it misses nuance because the query and the document never got to interact directly.

Re-ranking is the actual date: you take the query and each candidate document and run them through a model together, so the model can directly attend from query words to document words and vice versa, and score how relevant they really are to each other. That's way more expensive per pair, which is exactly why you don't do it against the whole corpus -- you only run it on the handful of candidates the cheap first pass already shortlisted.

So in this case, I wouldn't dump all 20 chunks into the LLM and hope it sorts out relevance itself -- I'd re-rank those 20 with a cross-encoder, keep maybe the top 3 to 5 by that more trustworthy score, and only put those into context. That directly fixes the buried-best-chunk problem, and it also just means less noisy, less redundant context for the model to reason over, which tends to improve answer quality on its own.
questions.example: Concretely: bi-encoder retrieval might rank a chunk about the refund policy for digital goods above one specifically about the refund policy for physical goods when the user asked about a physical item, because both score similarly in embedding space -- a cross-encoder re-ranker, seeing the query and both chunks together, can catch that distinction and flip the ranking.

Not explaining why bi-encoder retrieval misses query-document interaction signals
Assuming a cross-encoder re-ranker could replace the first-pass retrieval entirely without a scalability cost
Not recognizing that re-ranking is applied only to the narrowed candidate set, not the full corpus
Ignoring that reducing noisy or redundant context after re-ranking also improves answer quality independent of ranking order
keyPoints: First-pass retrieval uses independently computed query and document embeddings for cheap, scalable similarity search
This independence limits precision because the query and document never directly interact during embedding
A cross-encoder re-ranker jointly processes the query and each candidate, producing a far more precise relevance score
Re-ranking is applied only to the small shortlisted candidate set, balancing cost against precision
Re-ranking improves both ordering and the ability to drop mediocre chunks before context assembly, improving downstream answer quality

questions.title: What's Actually Happening in the ReAct Loop Between Model and Harness
questions.prompt: A teammate says their agent basically already does ReAct because it calls a function and uses the result in its reply. Explain the technical mechanics of the ReAct pattern -- the interleaving of reasoning traces and actions across multiple turns of the prompt/response loop between the model and the tool-calling harness -- and explain specifically why a single function call followed by one final reply does not qualify as ReAct.
questions.modelAnswer:
ReAct, short for Reasoning plus Acting, is a prompting and orchestration pattern where the model is explicitly induced to interleave verbalized reasoning steps with discrete actions across multiple rounds of a loop, rather than producing one reasoning block followed by one action followed immediately by a final answer. Mechanically, the orchestration code around the model, often called the harness, sends a prompt, the model emits a reasoning step and an action such as calling a specific tool with arguments, the harness executes that action against the real tool or environment, the result, often called an observation, is appended back into the conversation, and the augmented context is sent back to the model for another round. The model then reasons again, now conditioned on the new observation, and decides whether to take another action or produce a final answer.

The critical mechanical property is that each action's result becomes new input the model actually reasons over before deciding its next step, and the loop can repeat an arbitrary number of times depending on what the model encounters. If a tool call returns an unexpected or partial result, the model's next reasoning step explicitly incorporates that observation and can revise its plan, call a different tool, or retry with different arguments. This is what allows ReAct-style agents to recover from errors, handle multi-step tasks where the right next action depends on what an earlier action returned, and ground their reasoning in real intermediate feedback from the environment rather than reasoning purely from internal assumptions about what a tool would return.

A single function call followed immediately by a final reply doesn't qualify because there's no loop and no conditioning on an observation in subsequent reasoning -- it's a straight-line sequence of user input, one tool call, then formatting the result into a reply, with no branch point where the model re-reasons based on what actually came back and decides on a further action. If that one tool call fails or only partially answers the user's need, a true ReAct-style agent would feed that observation back in and let the model's next reasoning step decide what to do about it; the teammate's implementation has no mechanism for that because it never routes the tool result back through another round of model reasoning that can trigger a further action. It is tool-augmented generation, not an iterative reasoning-acting loop.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd push back on that framing directly, because the core thing that makes something ReAct isn't that it can call a tool -- plenty of systems do that. It's the loop: the model reasons, the model acts, the real result comes back, and that result gets fed back in so the model reasons again with that new information in hand, potentially acting again. One tool call and done isn't a loop, it's a single branch.

The mechanical detail I'd walk through is what the harness is actually doing between model calls: after the tool executes, the result gets appended to the conversation and sent back to the model as new context, and the model's next output is conditioned on that observation, not just on the original user request. That's the part that lets it recover when something goes wrong -- if the first tool call comes back empty or errors out, a real ReAct loop lets the model see that and decide to retry, try a different tool, or ask for clarification, instead of just blindly formatting whatever it got into a reply.

So I'd tell the teammate: what you've built is useful, tool-augmented generation is a completely valid pattern, but it's not ReAct unless there's an actual multi-round loop where observations can trigger further reasoning and further actions. The test I'd apply is: if the first tool call returns something unexpected, does your system have any path for the model to notice and react to that, or does it just move straight to a reply regardless? If it's the latter, there's no loop, so it's not ReAct.
questions.example: Minimal ReAct trace: reasoning step notes the order status is needed, action calls get_order with an id, the observation comes back as order not found, the next reasoning step concludes the id might be wrong and decides to ask the user to confirm it. A single-call system would have skipped straight from the failed lookup to an unconditioned reply.
commonMistakes: Equating any single tool call with implementing the ReAct pattern
Not describing the actual loop mechanics of reasoning, action, observation fed back, and repeat
Missing that the key property is the model reasoning over the observation before deciding its next step
Assuming ReAct requires a specific framework rather than being a prompting and orchestration pattern that can be implemented directly
Failing to explain why error recovery and multi-step adaptation require the loop structure, not a single call
keyPoints: ReAct interleaves verbalized reasoning with discrete actions across multiple rounds, not a single pass
The harness executes each action and appends the real result, the observation, back into the model's context
The model's next reasoning step is conditioned on that observation, enabling it to adapt its plan
The loop can repeat arbitrarily, allowing error recovery and multi-step task handling grounded in real feedback
A single tool call followed by a final reply lacks the loop and the re-reasoning-on-observation step, so it isn't ReAct

questions.title: Fixing a Prompt Template Where Few-Shot Examples Contradict the System Prompt
questions.prompt: A support-bot prompt template has a system prompt that says 'Always reply in the same language the customer used,' but every few-shot example in the template shows an English question followed by an English answer. In production, the bot replies in English even when customers write in Spanish or French. Rewrite the prompt template (including its variable substitution) so the few-shot examples reinforce the stated policy instead of silently overriding it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Few-shot examples are demonstrations, and models weight demonstrated behavior more heavily than declarative instructions when the two disagree -- the model is pattern-matching on 'what did the assistant actually do in the examples I was just shown,' not grading itself against the system prompt's wording. Here every single example is English-in/English-out, so the model learns 'this agent always answers in English' as a stronger, more recent signal than the one-line policy above it, and that pattern wins for non-English input. The fix isn't to delete the examples -- a support bot still benefits from seeing tone and format -- it's to make the examples actually demonstrate the rule being taught, not an unrelated default.

The corrected template needs at least one example where the input language and output language match and are not English, so the demonstration set itself encodes 'match the input language' rather than 'respond in English.' It also helps to keep the few-shot block short (two language pairs is enough) and to restate the invariant immediately before the live user turn, since instruction-following models weight the most recent system-level reminder more heavily than one stated far above several turns of context. Variable substitution should inject the user's message as its own turn, never concatenated into the few-shot block, so the model can't mistake it for another demonstration pair.

Finally, this needs a regression test, not just a visual read of the new template: run the same handful of non-English inputs through both the old and new prompt and assert the output script matches the input script (e.g. a language-detection check on the output), so the fix is verifiable and future prompt edits can be checked against it automatically rather than relying on someone noticing the bug again in production.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd point out to the team is that this isn't a prompt-wording bug, it's a demonstration bug -- the model is doing exactly what it was shown, not what it was told. Everyone's instinct is to make the system prompt stronger ('ALWAYS reply in the same language, no exceptions'), but that rarely moves the needle much because the few-shot examples are a much louder signal than a single instruction line. If every example you show the model is English-to-English, you've effectively taught it that English-to-English is the task, and the policy sentence becomes background noise.

So what I'd actually do is rewrite the few-shot set so it demonstrates the behavior I want, not just the tone I want. I'd swap one of the two examples for a Spanish-in/Spanish-out pair, keep one English pair, and now the pattern across the examples is 'match the customer's language' instead of 'answer in English.' I'd also move the policy reminder to sit right next to the live user turn rather than only at the very top, because in my experience recency matters a lock in multi-turn context -- the model weighs the instruction it saw most recently more than one it saw several messages back.

And I wouldn't ship that fix on faith. I'd write four or five test inputs in different languages, run them through the old template and the new one, and literally check that the output script matches the input -- something as simple as a regex on character ranges or a language-detection call is enough to catch regressions. That turns 'I think this fixed it' into a repeatable check I can rerun every time someone touches this prompt later.
commonMistakes: Only rewording the system prompt ('ALWAYS reply in the customer's language!') without touching the few-shot examples
Deleting the few-shot examples entirely instead of fixing what they demonstrate, losing the tone/format guidance they provided
Adding a non-English example but putting it last and leaving two English examples before it, so English still dominates the pattern
Concatenating the live user message into the few-shot block instead of passing it as a separate turn, confusing the model about what's a demonstration versus the real query
Shipping the fix without a regression test, so a future prompt edit can silently reintroduce the same bug
keyPoints: Identifies that few-shot demonstrations outweigh declarative instructions when they conflict
Rewrites the few-shot set to actually demonstrate the target behavior (language-matching), not just adjust wording
Keeps the few-shot block short and balanced rather than skewed toward one pattern
Places a reminder near the live user turn so recency reinforces the policy
Adds a concrete regression test that checks output language against input language

Rewrites few-shot examples to demonstrate the intended behavior

questions.title: Building an Automated Prompt Eval Set for Regression Testing
questions.prompt: Your team wants to change the system prompt for a document-summarization feature, but every past change has been judged only by someone eyeballing a few outputs, and regressions have slipped through twice. Design a small automated eval set (test cases with checkable properties, not exact-string matches) and the scoring logic needed to compare the old prompt against the new one before shipping.
questions.modelAnswer:
Exact-string matching doesn't work for generative outputs because two correct summaries can be worded completely differently, so the eval set has to check properties of the output rather than its literal text. For each test case I'd define: an input document, and a set of checkable assertions -- does the output mention required entities/facts (checked via substring or keyword presence, or a cheap NLI/entailment check), does it stay under a length budget, does it avoid a banned phrase or format violation, and optionally a rubric score from a separate LLM-as-judge call for subjective qualities like tone or coherence. Each assertion should be a small deterministic function so the suite runs without needing a human in the loop.

The eval set itself should be curated to cover the failure modes that matter: a short document, a very long document that forces truncation/compression, a document with a figure or table reference, a document with conflicting statements, and an edge case like empty or near-empty input. Each case stores expected_properties (e.g. must_contain, max_words, must_not_contain) rather than an expected string.

Scoring logic runs both the old and new prompt over every case, checks each assertion, and produces a pass/fail matrix plus an aggregate score per prompt version. The threshold for shipping is a policy decision (e.g. 'new prompt must not regress on any case that currently passes, and must improve or hold steady on aggregate score'), and the harness should print exactly which cases flipped from pass to fail so a reviewer can look at those specific outputs rather than rereading everything.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Whenever someone says 'we eyeballed a few outputs and it looked fine,' that's the point where I push back and say we need cases with checkable properties, because 'looked fine' doesn't scale and doesn't catch regressions on the cases nobody happened to glance at. So the first thing I do is sit down and write out five or six documents that represent the different ways this feature gets used -- a short announcement, a dense technical doc, something with a table, something with contradictory info -- and for each one I ask 'what would make this summary objectively wrong,' not 'what's the perfect summary.' That gives me assertions like 'must mention the renewal date' or 'must be under 80 words' instead of a golden string I'd have to match exactly.

Then I build a tiny harness: run the old prompt and the new prompt over all the cases, check each assertion, and print a diff -- which cases passed on the old prompt but fail on the new one. That diff is the whole point of the exercise; it's the thing that would have caught the two regressions that slipped through before, because instead of asking 'does this look okay,' I'm asking 'did we break anything that used to work.'

For the fuzzier qualities -- tone, coherence, whether the summary reads naturally -- I'll add an LLM-as-judge pass with a rubric, but I treat that as a secondary signal, not the primary gate, because judge models have their own biases and inconsistency. The hard assertions are what block a ship; the judge score is what I look at when the hard assertions all pass and I want a sanity check on quality before rolling out.
questions.example:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class EvalCase:
    name: str
    document: str
    must_contain: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    must_not_contain: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    max_words: int | None = None

EVAL_SET = [
    EvalCase(
        name="renewal_date_present",
        document="Your Acme Cloud subscription renews on 2026-11-15 at the Pro tier...",
        must_contain=["2026-11-15"],
        max_words=60,
    ),
    EvalCase(
        name="no_hallucinated_price",
        document="The outage lasted 40 minutes and affected the EU region only.",
        must_not_contain=["$", "refund"],
        max_words=50,
    ),
]

def score(summary: str, case: EvalCase) -> dict:
    words = len(summary.split())
    results = {
        "contains_required": all(k in summary for k in case.must_contain),
        "avoids_banned": not any(k in summary for k in case.must_not_contain),
        "within_length": case.max_words is None or words <= case.max_words,
    }
    results["passed"] = all(results.values())
    return results

def run_regression(old_prompt_fn, new_prompt_fn, cases=EVAL_SET):
    regressions = []
    for case in cases:
        old_pass = score(old_prompt_fn(case.document), case)["passed"]
        new_pass = score(new_prompt_fn(case.document), case)["passed"]
        if old_pass and not new_pass:
            regressions.append(case.name)
    return regressions  # ship only if this list is empty
commonMistakes: Writing eval cases as exact expected output strings, which breaks on any valid rewording
Only testing happy-path documents and skipping edge cases like empty input or conflicting facts
Relying solely on an LLM-as-judge score with no deterministic assertions, making the suite non-reproducible
Not diffing old-prompt vs. new-prompt results, so a case that regressed looks the same as one that was always failing
Hardcoding a pass threshold without defining what 'regression' means (e.g. shipping even though a previously-passing case now fails)
keyPoints: Uses checkable properties (contains/excludes/length) instead of exact string matches
Covers a deliberately varied set of edge cases, not just typical inputs
Runs old and new prompts over the same cases and diffs pass/fail results
Separates deterministic assertions (hard gate) from LLM-judge scoring (quality signal)
Defines an explicit ship/no-ship policy based on regressions, not just aggregate score

questions.title: Parsing a Final Answer Out of a Chain-of-Thought Trace Reliably
questions.prompt: A multi-step math/logic assistant uses chain-of-thought prompting, and the backend currently scrapes the 'final answer' by taking the last line of the model's free-text response. This breaks whenever the model adds a closing remark after its answer, or restates the answer mid-reasoning. Rewrite the prompt and parsing code so the final answer can be extracted reliably regardless of how much reasoning text surrounds it.
questions.code:
PROMPT = """Solve the problem step by step, then give the answer.

Problem: {problem}"""

def extract_answer(response_text: str) -> str:
    lines = response_text.strip().splitlines()
    return lines[-1]  # fragile: breaks on trailing remarks or restated answers
questions.modelAnswer:
Scraping free text for 'the answer' is fragile because there's no contract about where the answer lives -- the model might restate it inline, add a caveat after it, or format it differently each run. The fix is to make the prompt enforce a structural contract that both the model and the parser agree on, rather than hoping a heuristic like 'last line' holds. Chain-of-thought reasoning should still happen (it measurably improves accuracy on multi-step problems), but the final answer needs to be wrapped in an unambiguous, machine-parseable delimiter that only ever appears once and only around the answer.

A reliable pattern is to instruct the model to put its reasoning first, then emit a fixed tag like <answer>42</answer> or a JSON object on its own line as the very last thing in the response, and explicitly instruct it not to add anything after that tag. The parser then uses a regex anchored to that tag rather than positional heuristics like 'last line' or 'last number in the text,' so it doesn't care how much reasoning precedes it or whether the model restates the answer in prose beforehand.

It's also worth handling the failure case explicitly: if the regex finds zero or more than one match, that's a signal the model violated the contract, and the code should treat it as a retryable error (re-prompt, or fall back to a stricter structured-output mode) rather than silently guessing with a fallback heuristic that reintroduces the original fragility.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The bug here is that 'last line of the response' was never actually a contract, it just happened to work on the examples someone tested with. Chain-of-thought is genuinely useful -- it measurably helps the model get multi-step problems right -- so I don't want to drop it, I want to stop relying on positional guessing to find the answer inside it.

What I do is change the prompt so the model's output has an explicit, named slot for the final answer that it's told never to put anything else inside or after. Something like 'after your reasoning, output the final answer as <answer>...</answer> on its own line, and output nothing after that tag.' Then on the parsing side, I throw away any idea of 'the last line' and just regex for that tag specifically. It doesn't matter anymore if the model adds a closing remark, restates the number in a sentence above, or reasons for twenty lines -- the parser is looking for one specific, unambiguous marker.

The other thing I always add, because I've been burned by skipping it, is a check for the failure case: what if the tag isn't there, or shows up twice? I don't want the code to silently fall back to some other heuristic, because that's exactly how the original bug happened. I treat a missing or duplicated tag as a hard signal to retry the call or fall back to a stricter JSON-mode response, and I log it, because a model that regularly violates the output contract is a sign the prompt itself needs tightening, not that the parser needs another regex exception.
questions.example:
import re

PROMPT = """Solve the problem step by step. Show your reasoning.
Then, on its own line, output the final answer wrapped exactly like this:
<answer>VALUE</answer>
Output nothing after the closing tag.

Problem: {problem}"""

ANSWER_RE = re.compile(r"<answer>(.*?)</answer>", re.DOTALL)

def extract_answer(response_text: str) -> str:
    matches = ANSWER_RE.findall(response_text)
    if len(matches) != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Expected exactly one <answer> tag, found {len(matches)}. "
            "Retry the call or fall back to structured JSON mode."
        )
    return matches[0].strip()

# Example model output this correctly parses regardless of surrounding text:
# "First, 12 * 3 = 36. Then subtract 4: 36 - 4 = 32.\n<answer>32</answer>"
assert extract_answer(

questions.title: Writing a Semantic-Boundary-Aware Chunking Function for Document Ingestion
questions.prompt: Your RAG pipeline currently chunks documents by splitting every 500 characters with no regard for content, which regularly cuts sentences and code blocks in half and produces chunks that retrieve poorly. Write a chunking function for ingestion that respects semantic boundaries (sentences, paragraphs, and fenced code blocks) and still supports overlap between consecutive chunks for context continuity.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fixed-size character splitting treats the document as an opaque byte stream, so it has no concept of 'don't cut here' and will happily split a sentence, a bullet point, or a fenced code block in the middle. The fix is to chunk at structural boundaries first and only fall back to a size limit when a single structural unit is too large on its own. Concretely: split the document into paragraphs and fenced code blocks as atomic units (a code block between triple backticks is never split internally), then greedily pack consecutive units into a chunk until adding the next unit would exceed the target size, at which point the chunk is closed and a new one starts.

Overlap should be added at the unit level, not by re-slicing raw characters -- carry the last one or two sentences/paragraphs of the previous chunk into the start of the next chunk, so retrieval still benefits from continuity without reintroducing the mid-sentence problem. If an individual unit (e.g. a huge code block) genuinely exceeds the max chunk size on its own, that's the one case where a size-based fallback split is acceptable, and it should prefer splitting on blank lines or statement boundaries within that unit rather than an arbitrary character offset.

The resulting function takes a target chunk size and overlap size as parameters, uses a sentence/paragraph tokenizer (or a simple regex-based splitter if a full NLP library isn't warranted) to get atomic units, tracks fenced code blocks separately so backtick regions are never split, and packs/overlaps units rather than characters.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The giveaway that fixed-size chunking is wrong here is that it doesn't know what a sentence or a code fence is -- it's just slicing bytes. So the first change I make is to stop thinking in characters and start thinking in units: paragraphs, sentences, and code blocks as atomic things that never get split internally. I'll regex out fenced code blocks first and treat each one as a single indivisible unit, then split the remaining prose into paragraphs or sentences.

From there it's basically bin-packing: walk through the units in order, keep adding them to the current chunk, and as soon as the next unit would push you over the target size, close the chunk and start a new one. That guarantees every chunk boundary falls between units, never inside one, so you never get half a sentence or a dangling unclosed code fence.

For overlap, I don't re-slice characters from the end of the previous chunk -- I carry over the last unit or two, whole, into the start of the next chunk. That way the overlap is still a complete sentence or paragraph, not a fragment, and retrieval still gets the continuity benefit. The one place I allow a straight size-based cut is when a single unit -- usually a giant code block -- is larger than the entire target chunk size by itself; in that case I split on blank lines inside it rather than an arbitrary offset, because that's the only case where there's no better boundary available.
questions.example:
import re

CODE_FENCE_RE = re.compile(r"```.*?```", re.DOTALL)

def split_into_units(text: str) -> list[str]:
    units, last_end = [], 0
    for match in CODE_FENCE_RE.finditer(text):
        if match.start() > last_end:
            prose = text[last_end:match.start()]
            units.extend(p.strip() for p in re.split(r"\n\s*\n", prose) if p.strip())
        units.append(match.group())  # code block kept atomic
        last_end = match.end()
    if last_end < len(text):
        prose = text[last_end:]
        units.extend(p.strip() for p in re.split(r"\n\s*\n", prose) if p.strip())
    return units

def chunk_document(text: str, max_chars: int = 800, overlap_units: int = 1) -> list[str]:
    units = split_into_units(text)
    chunks, current, current_len = [], [], 0
    for unit in units:
        if current and current_len + len(unit) > max_chars:
            chunks.append("\n\n".join(current))
            current = current[-overlap_units:]  # carry whole units forward
            current_len = sum(len(u) for u in current)
        current.append(unit)
        current_len += len(unit)
    if current:
        chunks.append("\n\n".join(current))
    return chunks
