Implementing overlap by re-slicing characters from the previous chunk, reintroducing mid-sentence fragments
Splitting inside a fenced code block, leaving a dangling opening or closing backtick fence
Setting chunk size far too small for fenced code blocks, forcing a bad fallback split on every code-heavy document
Not handling the oversized-single-unit edge case at all, causing an infinite loop or a chunk that silently exceeds the max size
keyPoints: Treats fenced code blocks as atomic units that are never split internally
Splits prose into paragraph/sentence units before packing into chunks
Packs whole units into chunks up to the size limit rather than slicing raw characters
Implements overlap by carrying whole units forward, not re-slicing character ranges
Has an explicit, reasonable fallback for a single unit that exceeds the max chunk size on its own

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly avoids splitting fenced code blocks internally
Splits prose at sentence/paragraph boundaries rather than fixed character offsets
Implements overlap at the unit level, preserving whole sentences/paragraphs
Handles the oversized single-unit edge case sensibly
Produces working, correct code

questions.title: Implementing a Retrieve-then-Re-Rank Pipeline Before Prompt Assembly
questions.prompt: A RAG system currently takes the top-5 results straight from vector similarity search and drops them into the prompt, but relevant passages are frequently ranked 8th or 9th because embedding similarity alone doesn't capture fine-grained relevance. Write the retrieval code path that embeds the query, pulls a wider top-k candidate set from the vector store, and re-ranks those candidates with a cross-encoder-style scorer before selecting the final context to send to the LLM.
questions.code:
def retrieve(query: str, k: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    query_vec = embed(query)
    results = vector_store.search(query_vec, top_k=k)
    return [r.text for r in results]
# Problem: only ever looks at 5 candidates, no re-ranking.
questions.modelAnswer:
Embedding similarity is a fast, approximate relevance signal -- it compares a query vector against document vectors independently, so it can't model fine-grained interactions between the specific query and a specific passage the way a model that reads both together can. That's exactly why a passage can be semantically 'in the neighborhood' (rank 8-9) without being the best answer to the actual question. The standard fix is a two-stage retrieval: cast a wide net with the cheap vector search (e.g. top-30 or top-50), then run a more expensive but more accurate cross-encoder-style scorer that takes the (query, passage) pair jointly and reorders by that score, finally truncating to the small number that actually goes into the prompt (e.g. top-5).

The vector search stage should retrieve meaningfully more candidates than the final context size -- often 5-10x -- because the whole point is to give the re-ranker a wide enough pool that the true best passages are likely inside it, even if they didn't make the embedding-only top-5. The re-ranker scores each (query, candidate) pair independently (or via a cross-encoder's joint-encoding forward pass) and the candidates are sorted by that score, not by the original vector-similarity score.

Practically, this means two separate scoring functions in the pipeline, and it's important the final context assembly uses the re-ranked order, not the original vector order -- a common bug is re-ranking into a new list but then forgetting to use it, silently keeping the old top-5.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The mental model I use here is 'cheap and wide, then expensive and narrow.' Vector similarity is fast enough to search over millions of chunks, but it's a blunt instrument -- it's comparing two vectors independently, with no idea what the actual query is asking versus what the passage actually says in context. So I never expect the embedding search alone to put the single best passage at rank 1; I expect it to put the best passages somewhere in the top 30 or 50, and that's the assumption the whole design rests on.

So the pipeline becomes two stages. First, vector search pulls a wide candidate pool -- I'll usually grab 6-10x more candidates than I actually plan to use. Then I run those candidates through a re-ranker that actually looks at the query and the passage together -- a cross-encoder, or a reranking API if I don't want to host the model myself -- and that joint scoring is what decides the final order, not the original cosine similarity.

The bug I watch for every time I build this, because I've shipped it by accident before, is forgetting to actually use the re-ranked list downstream -- you compute re-ranked scores, sort them into a new list, and then some other part of the code still reads from the original vector-search results. So I make the re-ranker's output the only thing that gets passed into prompt assembly, and I'll usually log both rankings side by side while testing so I can see the re-ranker actually moved things, instead of silently agreeing with the vector order every time.
questions.example:
def embed(text: str) -> list[float]:
    ...  # calls embedding model

def cross_encoder_score(query: str, passage: str) -> float:
    ...  # joint (query, passage) relevance score, e.g. ms-marco cross-encoder

def retrieve_and_rerank(query: str, candidate_k: int = 40, final_k: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    query_vec = embed(query)
    candidates = vector_store.search(query_vec, top_k=candidate_k)
    candidate_texts = [r.text for r in candidates]

    scored = [
        (text, cross_encoder_score(query, text))
        for text in candidate_texts
    ]
    scored.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)  # re-ranked order

    return [text for text, _ in scored[:final_k]]  # final_k uses RE-RANKED order

def assemble_prompt(query: str) -> str:
    context_chunks = retrieve_and_rerank(query)
    context = "\n\n---\n\n".join(context_chunks)
    return f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {query}"
commonMistakes: Retrieving only as many candidates from the vector store as will be used in the final prompt, giving the re-ranker nothing extra to work with
Re-ranking into a new sorted list but then feeding the original vector-search order into the final prompt
Using the embedding similarity score instead of the cross-encoder score to sort the final results
Running the cross-encoder over too many candidates (e.g. hundreds), creating unnecessary latency without improving the final top-k
Not re-ranking at all and assuming a higher vector top-k alone fixes relevance ordering
keyPoints: Retrieves a candidate pool meaningfully larger than the final context size
Uses a cross-encoder-style scorer that jointly considers the query and passage, not just embedding similarity
Sorts final results by the re-ranker's score, not the original vector-search score
Ensures prompt assembly reads from the re-ranked list, not the original candidates
Balances candidate pool size against re-ranking latency/cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Implements a two-stage pipeline: wide vector search then re-ranking
Correctly scores (query, passage) pairs jointly for re-ranking
Final context selection uses the re-ranked order, not the original vector order
Chooses a sensible candidate pool size relative to the final top-k
Clean, correct, runnable code

questions.title: Configuring Hybrid Metadata-Filtered Vector Search
questions.prompt: A legal-document assistant's RAG pipeline is returning relevant-looking passages from contracts that have since been superseded or that belong to the wrong client, because the vector query only looks at embedding similarity. Configure a vector database query that combines vector similarity search with a metadata predicate (e.g. client_id match and status = 'active', filtered to documents from the last 2 years) so retrieval is both semantically and factually correct.
questions.modelAnswer:
Pure vector similarity has no notion of business rules like 'this document was superseded' or 'this belongs to a different client' -- it only measures semantic closeness, so a stale or wrong-tenant document can easily out-score the correct one if its wording happens to be closer to the query. The fix is to attach structured metadata to every indexed chunk at ingestion time (client_id, status, effective_date or last_modified) and pass a metadata filter alongside the vector in every query, so the vector database only considers candidates that satisfy the predicate before ranking by similarity.

Most production vector databases support this as a native 'filtered search' -- the filter is applied either as a pre-filter (restrict the candidate set, then do similarity search within it) or as a post-filter (search broadly, then discard non-matching results), and the two have different correctness/performance tradeoffs: pre-filtering guarantees correctness but can be slower on some index types if the filter is very selective, while post-filtering is faster but risks returning fewer than top_k results if too many top matches get filtered out, which means you may need to over-fetch (e.g. ask for 3-5x top_k) before filtering.

For this scenario specifically, the filter should combine an exact-match predicate (client_id == the requesting client, status == 'active') with a range predicate (effective_date >= now - 2 years), and all of that should be enforced at the database query level, not fetched broadly and filtered in application code after the fact, both for correctness (don't want top_k consumed by documents that get discarded) and for data isolation (a client's documents should never even be retrieved for another client, not just filtered out afterward on the client side).
questions.professionalAnswer:
The moment I hear 'wrong client's documents showed up,' my first reaction is that this isn't a ranking quality problem, it's a data isolation problem -- the vector search never should have been looking at those documents in the first place. Pure cosine similarity doesn't know what a client ID is, so if I don't tell the database to exclude other clients' data, it's going to happily return whatever's closest in meaning, security boundary or not.

So the way I build this is: at ingestion, every chunk gets metadata -- client_id, status, effective_date -- stored alongside the vector, not bolted on afterward. Then at query time, I pass both the query vector and a filter expression together into one call to the vector database, so filtering happens inside the search itself, not as a second pass in my application code after I've already pulled back results.

One thing I always check with whatever vector database I'm using is whether the filter is applied before or after the similarity ranking. If it filters after, and I only asked for top_k=5, I could end up with fewer than 5 usable results if several of the top similarity matches get thrown out -- so I'll over-fetch, say top_k=25, apply the filter, then truncate to the 5 I actually want. And for something like client isolation specifically, I treat that as a hard pre-filter, not an optional nice-to-have, because 'faster but occasionally leaks another client's document' isn't an acceptable tradeoff here.
commonMistakes: Filtering results in application code after fetching a fixed top_k, instead of filtering at the database query level
Not storing the metadata needed for filtering at ingestion time, making correct filtering impossible later
Treating client_id isolation as a post-filter instead of a hard pre-filter, risking a data leak between clients
Requesting only top_k candidates when the database applies filters after similarity ranking, resulting in fewer usable results than needed
Using a loose date comparison (string comparison instead of a proper date type) that silently misorders or excludes valid documents
keyPoints: Stores structured metadata (client_id, status, effective_date) on every chunk at ingestion time
Combines the metadata filter with the vector query in a single database-level call
Understands the pre-filter vs. post-filter tradeoff for the specific vector database in use
Over-fetches top_k when filtering may be applied after ranking, to avoid under-returning results
Treats data-isolation predicates (like client_id) as a hard filter, not an optional refinement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly combines vector search with a metadata filter at the database query level
Designs correct metadata schema stored at ingestion time
Explains/handles the pre-filter vs. post-filter tradeoff appropriately
Treats client isolation as a hard filter rather than application-side cleanup
Clean, correct, runnable query code

questions.title: Building a RAG Evaluation Harness for Faithfulness and Retrieval Quality
questions.prompt: Your team suspects the RAG assistant is sometimes answering confidently with information that isn't actually in the retrieved context (hallucinating on top of retrieval), but there's no way to measure this today beyond spot-checking. Write a small evaluation harness that scores faithfulness (is the generated answer supported by the retrieved context) and retrieval precision/recall against a labeled eval set of questions with known relevant document IDs.
questions.modelAnswer:
This requires two genuinely different measurements that get conflated too often: retrieval quality (did the system fetch the right documents) and faithfulness (did the generated answer stick to what those documents actually say). Retrieval precision/recall is straightforward and deterministic given a labeled eval set: each question has a set of known-relevant document IDs, and for a given query you compute precision as (retrieved docs that are relevant) / (total retrieved) and recall as (retrieved docs that are relevant) / (total relevant), aggregated across the eval set, typically at a fixed k.

Faithfulness is harder because it's a semantic property of the generated answer relative to the retrieved context, not relative to ground truth -- an answer can be faithful (fully supported by context) and still wrong if the retrieved context itself was bad, which is exactly why these two metrics must be reported separately rather than collapsed into one 'RAG score.' A practical faithfulness check decomposes the generated answer into its individual claims (sentence-level is usually good enough) and asks a judge model, given only the retrieved context, whether each claim is entailed by, contradicted by, or unsupported by that context -- this is itself a form of LLM-as-judge, so it needs its own calibration (spot-check judge verdicts against human labels on a sample) rather than being trusted blindly.

The harness runs the full pipeline (retrieve, then generate) per eval question, logs retrieved doc IDs against the labeled relevant set for precision/recall, and separately runs the faithfulness judge against (generated answer, retrieved context) pairs, reporting both metrics per-question and aggregated, so a regression in retrieval versus a regression in generation faithfulness can be told apart.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing I want to nail down first, before writing any code, is that 'is the RAG system good' is actually two separate questions: did it find the right documents, and did it stick to what those documents said. Teams love to collapse this into one fuzzy 'quality' number, but that makes debugging impossible -- if the final answer is wrong, you need to know whether retrieval failed or generation hallucinated on top of good retrieval, and those get fixed in completely different places.

For retrieval, I keep it boring and deterministic: I need a labeled eval set where each question already has the correct document IDs attached, and then it's just precision and recall at whatever k I'm retrieving -- how many of what I pulled back were actually relevant, and how many of the relevant ones did I actually pull back. No LLM needed for that part at all.

Faithfulness is the harder, fuzzier one, because I'm asking 'does this specific sentence in the answer actually follow from this specific context,' and that's a judgment call I delegate to a judge model -- I'll break the answer into individual claims and ask the judge, for each claim, whether it's supported by the retrieved context, not by the judge's own world knowledge. And because I'm using a model to grade a model, I don't trust it blindly -- I'll pull a sample of those judge verdicts and have a human check them before I trust the aggregate faithfulness score. Then I report retrieval metrics and faithfulness metrics as two separate numbers per question, because that separation is the whole point -- it tells me whether to go fix the retriever or go fix the prompt.
commonMistakes: Collapsing retrieval quality and generation faithfulness into a single score, making regressions impossible to localize
Measuring faithfulness against ground-truth facts instead of against the retrieved context the model actually had
Scoring faithfulness at the whole-answer level instead of per-claim, missing partial hallucination inside an otherwise-correct answer
Trusting the LLM-judge's faithfulness verdicts with no human-sample calibration
Computing precision/recall without a fixed k, making results incomparable across runs
keyPoints: Separates retrieval metrics (precision/recall vs. labeled relevant docs) from faithfulness metrics (answer vs. retrieved context)
Computes precision and recall correctly against a labeled eval set
Scores faithfulness at the claim level, not just the whole-answer level
Judges faithfulness against the retrieved context, not external ground truth
Calibrates or spot-checks the LLM-judge against human judgment rather than trusting it blindly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements retrieval precision/recall against labeled relevant docs
Implements a reasonable per-claim faithfulness scoring approach
Correctly distinguishes faithfulness (vs. context) from correctness (vs. ground truth)
Addresses calibration/reliability of the LLM-judge
Clean, working harness code that reports both metrics per question

questions.title: Fixing an Ambiguous Tool Schema for Agent Function Calling
questions.prompt: An agent has a tool called update_record with parameters record and value, both typed as free-form strings, and in practice the model frequently calls it with the wrong field updated, malformed IDs, or missing required context because the schema gives it almost nothing to work with. Rewrite the tool schema with proper typing, required fields, enums where applicable, and descriptions precise enough that the model can call it correctly and the backend can validate the call before executing it.
questions.modelAnswer:
This schema fails because it describes almost nothing about the tool's actual contract -- 'record' as a bare string gives the model no signal about what identifies a record (an ID? a name? which table?), and 'value' as a bare string means the model has to guess both which field to change and what format the new value should be in, with no required fields enforced at all. A well-designed schema needs to make the implicit structure explicit: separate parameters for record_id (typed and pattern-constrained, e.g. a UUID or a known ID format), field (constrained to an enum of the actual updatable fields), and new_value (typed appropriately per field, or at minimum documented with examples and format constraints), with record_id and field marked required.

Descriptions matter as much as types here -- each parameter description should state exactly what the model needs to know to fill it correctly: where record_id comes from (e.g. 'the id field returned by search_records, not a display name'), what field values are valid (the enum does this structurally), and what new_value should look like for each field (e.g. 'for field=status, new_value must be one of: open, in_progress, closed'). This is also a case where splitting one ambiguous tool into more constrained tools can help -- e.g. update_record_status(record_id, status: enum) separate from update_record_owner(record_id, owner_email) -- trading a little duplication for parameters that are unambiguous and independently validatable, which matters most for high-risk fields.

Finally, the backend should validate the call against the schema's constraints before executing -- reject an unknown field value, reject a record_id that doesn't match the expected pattern -- rather than relying on the model having gotten it right, because schema constraints at the LLM layer reduce but don't eliminate malformed calls.
questions.professionalAnswer:
When I see a tool with two bare string parameters called 'record' and 'value,' my read is that the model is being asked to guess at least three things at once -- what identifies the record, which field is being changed, and what format the new value needs to be in -- and nobody designed the schema to answer any of those questions for it. So the fix starts with naming and typing: record_id as its own parameter, with a description that says exactly where that ID comes from, because 'record' could mean a name, a slug, or a UUID and the model has no way to know which.

Then I'd pull 'which field' out into its own parameter and make it an enum of the actual updatable fields, because an enum is a structural guarantee -- the model literally cannot pass a field that doesn't exist, versus a free-text field name where it might pass 'Status' or 'state' or something close but wrong. And for new_value, I either tie its format to the chosen field in the description, or honestly, if a couple of fields are high-risk (like status changes that trigger workflows), I'll just split those into their own dedicated tools -- update_record_status(record_id, status: enum) -- so the schema itself rules out an invalid combination instead of relying on a description to explain it.

And I never treat the schema as the only line of defense. Even with good typing, I validate the actual tool call server-side before executing it -- check the record_id format, check the field/value combination makes sense -- because schemas reduce bad calls, they don't guarantee against them, and the blast radius of a wrong update_record call is exactly the kind of thing I want a second check on before it touches real data.
commonMistakes: Leaving identifier and value parameters as untyped free strings with no format constraints
Not using an enum for a field that has a small, known set of valid values
Writing a one-line description ('Updates a record.') that gives the model no guidance on correct usage
Not marking critical parameters as required, letting the model omit them and the backend guess defaults
Relying on the schema alone for safety instead of also validating the actual call server-side before execution
keyPoints: Replaces ambiguous free-string parameters with properly typed, named parameters
Uses enums for parameters with a known, bounded set of valid values
Writes descriptions precise enough to tell the model exactly where values come from and what format is expected
Marks required parameters explicitly in the schema
Adds server-side validation of the tool call in addition to schema-level constraints

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Redesigns parameters with correct, specific types instead of bare strings
Uses enums appropriately for bounded-value fields
Writes precise, actionable parameter and tool descriptions
Correctly marks required fields and addresses the ambiguity in the original schema
Mentions or implements server-side validation beyond the schema

questions.title: Implementing a Robust Agent Tool-Calling Loop
questions.prompt: An agent's current tool-calling code assumes the model's tool call always succeeds and always returns clean JSON, so a single malformed call or a tool-side exception crashes the whole request instead of letting the agent recover. Implement the tool-calling loop: parse the tool call out of the model's response, execute it, handle a tool error gracefully, and feed the result (success or error) back into the next model call so the agent can retry or adjust.
questions.code:
def run_agent(messages, tools):
    response = call_model(messages, tools)
    tool_call = response.tool_calls[0]
    args = json.loads(tool_call.arguments)
    result = execute_tool(tool_call.name, args)
    messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": result})
    return call_model(messages, tools)
# Problem: no error handling, assumes exactly one tool call, assumes valid JSON.
questions.modelAnswer:
The core issue is that this loop treats every step as guaranteed to succeed -- the model always calls a tool, the arguments are always valid JSON, the tool always executes without raising, and there's always exactly one call to handle. A correct loop has to treat each of those as a possible failure point and feed the failure back to the model as information, not let it propagate as an unhandled exception. Parsing the tool call's arguments should be wrapped so a JSON decode error produces a tool-result message describing the parse failure, not a crash -- the model can often self-correct on the next turn if told its arguments didn't parse.

Executing the tool itself needs a try/except boundary around the actual tool function, catching both expected domain errors (e.g. 'record not found') and unexpected exceptions, and in both cases constructing a tool-result message that reports success=false and an error description rather than letting the exception bubble up through the agent loop. The model needs that error fed back into the next call so it can decide whether to retry with different arguments, call a different tool, or give up and tell the user -- that decision belongs to the model/orchestration logic, not to the code crashing before the model gets a turn to react.

The loop also needs to handle zero or multiple tool calls in a single response (many APIs allow parallel tool calls), and it needs a termination condition -- a max iteration count or a check for an assistant message with no further tool calls -- so a model that keeps calling tools in an error loop doesn't run forever.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing that jumps out immediately is that every single step in this loop assumes the happy path -- valid JSON, a tool that never throws, exactly one tool call. In practice all three of those assumptions break eventually, and right now when any of them breaks, the whole request just dies instead of giving the agent a chance to recover.

So I wrap the risky parts individually. Parsing the arguments goes in a try/except, and if JSON decoding fails, I don't crash -- I build a tool-result message that says 'your arguments didn't parse as valid JSON' and feed that back to the model, because more often than not the model can fix its own malformed call on the next turn if you just tell it what went wrong. Same thing around actually executing the tool: anything the tool raises gets caught, turned into a structured error result, and handed back, rather than letting an exception from, say, a downstream API call take down the whole agent loop.

Then there's the stuff that's easy to forget because the original code just assumes it away: some APIs let the model request multiple tool calls in one turn, so I loop over all of them, not just tool_calls[0]. And I always put a hard cap on the number of iterations, because once you're feeding tool errors back into the conversation, it's completely possible for a model to get stuck retrying the same broken call over and over, and I'd rather the loop bail out after N attempts and surface that to a human than spin forever.
commonMistakes: Not wrapping JSON argument parsing, letting a malformed call crash the whole request instead of informing the model
Not catching exceptions raised by the tool itself, letting a downstream failure propagate as an unhandled error
Only handling tool_calls[0], silently dropping additional parallel tool calls in the same response
Feeding back a bare error string instead of a structured, consistent result format the model can reliably parse across turns
No iteration cap, allowing a stuck agent to retry the same failing call indefinitely
keyPoints: Wraps argument parsing so malformed JSON produces a tool-result error instead of crashing
Catches tool execution errors and converts them into structured results fed back to the model
Handles zero, one, or multiple tool calls per model response correctly
Feeds success and failure results back into the conversation in a consistent format
Enforces a maximum iteration count to prevent infinite retry loops

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly handles malformed tool-call arguments without crashing
Catches and gracefully reports tool execution errors
Correctly handles multiple/zero tool calls per response, not just the first
Feeds results (success or failure) back into the next model call consistently
Implements a termination/iteration-cap condition

questions.title: Implementing a Human-in-the-Loop Approval Gate for Destructive Agent Actions
questions.prompt: An agent with a delete_customer_data tool currently executes any tool call the model proposes immediately, which is fine for read-only lookups but dangerous for destructive actions. Implement an approval gate so that when the agent proposes a destructive action, execution pauses, the proposed action and its parameters are logged and surfaced for explicit human approval, and the agent only proceeds (or is told no) after a decision is recorded.
questions.modelAnswer:
The fix requires separating 'the model proposed an action' from 'the action was executed,' with an explicit, auditable decision point in between for anything destructive. Practically, each tool needs a declared risk tier (e.g. a requires_approval flag on the tool registry entry), and the execution path branches on that tier: a read-only or low-risk tool executes immediately as before, but a tool marked as requiring approval produces a pending-action record instead of running -- capturing the tool name, the exact arguments, the requesting session/user, and a timestamp -- and returns control without calling the underlying function.

That pending record needs to be durable (stored, not just held in memory) so an approval can come from a different process or a human reviewing a queue asynchronously, and the approval decision itself needs to be logged with who approved or rejected it and when, which is what makes the gate auditable rather than just a pause. Only after an explicit 'approved' decision is recorded does the code path that actually calls the destructive function run; a rejection (or an expiry/timeout) must route back into the agent loop as a tool result saying the action was denied, not as a silent no-op, so the model knows to stop retrying or to inform the user.

It's worth explicitly handling the case where the model proposes the same destructive action again after a rejection -- the gate should still require fresh approval rather than remembering an old approval for a structurally identical call, since parameters or circumstances may have changed between proposals.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The design principle I start from is: the model proposing an action and the system executing it need to be two separate steps, with a real decision point in between, whenever the action is destructive. Right now there's no such boundary -- the moment the model calls delete_customer_data, it just runs -- so the first thing I do is tag tools with a risk tier in the registry, something as simple as requires_approval: true, so the execution path can branch on it.

For anything tagged as requiring approval, instead of calling the function, I write a pending-action record somewhere durable -- a database row, not an in-memory variable -- with the exact tool name, the exact arguments, who or what requested it, and a timestamp. That's the artifact a human reviews. I don't execute anything until there's an explicit approval decision recorded against that pending record, and I log that decision too -- who approved it, when -- because 'we paused and then it ran' isn't enough; I want an audit trail that shows a specific person said yes to this specific action.

The part people forget is what happens on rejection, or if nobody responds. I make sure a rejection comes back into the agent's conversation as an explicit 'this action was denied' tool result, not nothing, so the model doesn't just hang or silently retry forever -- it needs to know to stop and tell the user, or try a different approach. And if the model proposes the exact same destructive call again later, I don't let a stale approval cover it; every proposal gets its own fresh approval record, because I don't want an old yes silently authorizing a new, possibly different situation.
commonMistakes: Executing the destructive tool immediately and only logging it afterward, instead of gating execution on a prior decision
Holding the pending-action record only in memory, making asynchronous/out-of-process approval impossible
Not recording who approved or rejected the action and when, leaving no real audit trail
Silently no-op'ing on rejection instead of feeding an explicit denial back into the agent's conversation
Reusing a previous approval for a new, structurally identical proposal instead of requiring fresh approval each time
keyPoints: Separates proposing an action from executing it, with a real decision point in between for destructive tools
Tags tools with a risk tier/approval requirement rather than treating all tools uniformly
Persists pending-action and decision records durably, not just in memory
Logs who made the approval/rejection decision and when, for auditability
Feeds a rejection back into the agent loop as an explicit denial rather than a silent no-op

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly gates destructive tool execution behind an explicit approval step
Designs a durable, auditable pending-action/decision record
Logs who approved/rejected and when
Handles rejection by feeding an explicit denial back to the agent, not a silent no-op
Clean, correct, runnable implementation

questions.title: Writing a Multi-Stage Dockerfile That Keeps a Python AI Image Small
questions.prompt: A team's Dockerfile for a Python inference service installs build tools, compiles dependencies, and copies a 4GB model-weights file in a single stage, producing a 9GB final image where most of that size is build-time cruft that serves no purpose at runtime. Rewrite the Dockerfile as a multi-stage build that separates build dependencies from the runtime image and handles the large model-weights file without baking an unnecessary copy of it into an intermediate layer.
questions.code:
FROM python:3.11
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential gcc
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY model-weights.bin /app/model-weights.bin
COPY . /app
CMD ["python", "/app/serve.py"]
# Problem: build tools and full dev image ship to production; single stage.
questions.modelAnswer:
A single-stage build bakes everything used at any point during the build -- compilers, headers, package caches, intermediate artifacts -- into the final image, because Docker layers are additive and nothing gets removed just because it's no longer needed. The fix is a multi-stage build: an early 'builder' stage installs build-essential, gcc, and compiles any packages that need native extensions, producing wheel files or an installed virtualenv, and a separate final stage starts from a minimal base image (e.g. python:3.11-slim) and copies only the already-built artifacts from the builder stage, never the build tools themselves.

For the model-weights file specifically, the layer-caching mechanism means a COPY of a large file becomes a permanent part of whichever layer it's copied in, even if a later layer in the same stage doesn't need it anymore -- so it should be copied directly into the final runtime stage (not the builder stage) and ideally only once, as close to the end of the Dockerfile as practical so it doesn't invalidate earlier cached layers on every code change. An even better pattern for genuinely large weights is to not bake them into the image at all -- mount them from a volume or pull them at container startup from object storage -- since a multi-gigabyte image is slow to push, pull, and scale regardless of how clean the build stages are; but if baking them in is required, they belong exclusively in the final stage.

The resulting Dockerfile should produce a final image containing only the Python runtime, installed dependencies (as wheels or a copied virtualenv), application code, and the model weights -- with zero compilers, zero apt package caches, and zero intermediate build artifacts.
questions.professionalAnswer:
When I look at a 9GB image for what should be a Python inference service, my first assumption is that the build tools never left the image -- gcc, build-essential, apt's package cache, all of that gets laid down as a layer and Docker has no way of knowing it's 'done being useful' once pip install finishes, so it just sits there forever.

The standard fix is splitting the Dockerfile into stages. I'll have a builder stage that's allowed to be messy -- install build-essential, gcc, compile whatever needs native extensions, maybe build wheels or populate a virtualenv -- and then a second, final stage that starts completely fresh from a slim base image and only copies over the specific artifacts I actually need from the builder: the installed packages, not the compiler that built them.

The model-weights file needs its own thought separately from that. If I copy it in the builder stage, it's now permanently part of a layer that gets rebuilt or recopied every time I touch the Dockerfile, even though the builder stage doesn't need those weights at all -- it's not training or compiling against them. So that COPY belongs only in the final stage, and I put it late in the Dockerfile so changing application code earlier doesn't force Docker to redo that large copy from cache. And honestly, for a 4GB file, I'd also raise the question of whether it should be in the image at all -- pulling it from object storage at container startup, or mounting it as a volume, often beats baking it in, because a multi-gigabyte image is painful to push and pull regardless of how clean the rest of the build is.
questions.example:
# ---- Stage 1: builder ----
FROM python:3.11 AS builder
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential gcc
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

# ---- Stage 2: runtime ----
FROM python:3.11-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app

# Only the compiled wheels, no compilers, no apt cache
COPY --from=builder /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels

COPY . /app

# Model weights copied only into the final stage, kept late to preserve
# Docker layer caching for earlier, more frequently-changed layers.
COPY model-weights.bin /app/model-weights.bin

CMD ["python", "serve.py"]
commonMistakes: Using a single stage so build tools (gcc, build-essential) remain in the final image
Copying the model-weights file into the builder stage instead of the final runtime stage
Not using a slim/minimal base image for the final stage, keeping unnecessary OS packages
Placing the large weights COPY early in the Dockerfile, invalidating its cached layer on every unrelated code change
Leaving apt/pip caches uncleaned in the final stage, adding avoidable size
keyPoints: Splits the Dockerfile into a builder stage and a minimal final runtime stage
Copies only built artifacts (wheels/installed packages) from the builder stage, never the compilers themselves
Copies the model-weights file only into the final stage, not the builder stage
Orders layers so large/rarely-changing copies don't invalidate caching unnecessarily
Uses a slim base image and cleans caches to minimize final image size

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements a multi-stage build separating build and runtime dependencies
Places the model-weights COPY correctly in the final stage only
Uses an appropriately minimal final base image
Orders Dockerfile layers sensibly for caching
Produces a correct, buildable Dockerfile overall

questions.title: Writing a Docker Compose File for an AI App With Secrets Handled Correctly
questions.prompt: A docker-compose.yml for an AI application has the OpenAI API key and database password hardcoded directly into the API service's environment block, and the compose file is checked into version control. Rewrite the docker-compose.yml so the API, vector database, and cache services are correctly wired together, and all secrets are supplied without ever being hardcoded in the committed file.
questions.code:
version: "3.9"
services:
  api:
    build: ./api
    environment:
      OPENAI_API_KEY: sk-live-abc123XYZ
      DATABASE_PASSWORD: sup3rSecret!
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
# Problem: secrets hardcoded and committed; no vector DB or cache service wired in.
questions.modelAnswer:
Hardcoding secrets directly into a compose file that's committed to version control means the secret is now permanently in git history, visible to anyone with repo access, and effectively impossible to fully rotate out without rewriting history -- it has to be removed from the file entirely and sourced at runtime instead. The standard mechanism is an env_file pointing at a .env file that is itself gitignored, or compose's native secrets: block backed by files outside the repo, with the compose file referencing variable names (${OPENAI_API_KEY}) rather than literal values -- the actual value lives only in the untracked .env file or the host/orchestrator's secret store, never in anything committed.

The multi-service wiring needs each service reachable by the others via compose's internal DNS (service name as hostname), explicit depends_on so the API doesn't start trying to connect before the vector database and cache are up, and named volumes for anything that needs to persist across container restarts (vector DB data, cache data if persistence is desired). Port mappings to the host should be minimized to only what actually needs external access -- the API, typically -- while the vector database and cache stay reachable only on the internal compose network unless there's a specific reason to expose them.

A .env.example file (with placeholder values, not real secrets) should be committed so other developers know which variables are required, while the actual .env file with real values is listed in .gitignore and never committed -- that combination is what actually solves the problem, not just moving the secret syntax around within the same committed file.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Seeing a live API key sitting in a docker-compose.yml that's checked into git is the kind of thing I'd flag immediately, because the damage is already done the moment it's committed -- that key is in git history now, and swapping it out of the current file doesn't remove it from history, so step one in real life would be rotating that key, not just fixing the file.

For the fix itself, I pull every secret out of the compose file and replace it with a variable reference, ${OPENAI_API_KEY} and so on, and those values get supplied through a .env file that sits next to the compose file but is explicitly gitignored. I'll commit a .env.example alongside it with placeholder values so anyone cloning the repo knows exactly which variables they need to set, without ever seeing a real secret.

Then for the actual multi-service wiring, I lean on what compose gives me for free: services can reach each other by service name over the internal network, so the API talks to the vector database and the cache using their service names as hostnames, not localhost and not hardcoded IPs. I add depends_on so the API doesn't race ahead and try to connect before the database container is actually ready, I give the vector database a named volume so its data survives a restart, and I'm deliberate about which ports actually get published to the host -- the API needs one, but the vector DB and cache have no business being reachable from outside the compose network unless I have a specific debugging reason to expose them temporarily.
questions.example:
# docker-compose.yml (committed)
version: "3.9"
services:
  api:
    build: ./api
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://app:${DATABASE_PASSWORD}@cache:5432/app
    depends_on:
      - vectordb
      - cache
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"

  vectordb:
    image: qdrant/qdrant:v1.9.0
    volumes:
      - vectordb_data:/qdrant/storage
    # no host port published -- only reachable inside the compose network

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    volumes:
      - cache_data:/data

volumes:
  vectordb_data:
  cache_data:

# .env (gitignored, NOT committed)
# OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-live-abc123XYZ
# DATABASE_PASSWORD=sup3rSecret!

# .env.example (committed, placeholders only)
# OPENAI_API_KEY=your-openai-key-here
# DATABASE_PASSWORD=your-db-password-here
commonMistakes: Only moving the secret value elsewhere in the same committed file instead of removing it from version control entirely
Forgetting to gitignore the actual .env file, committing real secret values anyway
Not rotating a secret that was previously committed, leaving it valid in git history
Publishing host ports for internal-only services (vector DB, cache) with no need for external access
Omitting depends_on, letting the API attempt connections before dependent services are ready
keyPoints: Removes all hardcoded secrets from the committed compose file
Uses env_file/.env (gitignored) or a secrets store, referenced via variables in the compose file
Commits a .env.example with placeholders so required variables are discoverable
Wires services together via compose's internal network/service-name DNS
Minimizes published host ports and adds depends_on/volumes appropriately

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly removes hardcoded secrets and sources them via env_file/variables
Ensures the actual secret file is gitignored, with a safe .env.example committed
Correctly wires API, vector database, and cache services together
Appropriately restricts published ports and uses depends_on/volumes
Valid, correct docker-compose.yml syntax

questions.title: Configuring Autoscaling for a Model-Serving Container to Handle Cold Starts
questions.prompt: A model-serving deployment currently scales from zero replicas and uses CPU-utilization-based autoscaling, so every traffic burst after an idle period produces 30-60 seconds of request timeouts while the large model loads into memory on a freshly started container. Write an autoscaling configuration (deployment manifest / scaling policy snippet) that accounts for this cold-start cost -- covering minimum replica count, scale-up triggers, and warm-pool reasoning.
questions.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: model-server
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: model-server
  minReplicas: 0
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
questions.modelAnswer:
Scaling to zero is the direct cause of the timeout window: with zero warm replicas, the first request after idle has to wait for a full cold start -- container scheduling, image pull if not cached, and critically, loading a large model's weights into memory (and onto GPU if applicable) -- before it can serve anything, and CPU-utilization-based scaling makes this worse because CPU usage during model loading often doesn't look like 'high load' to the autoscaler, so it may not even trigger additional scale-up quickly. The fix starts with minReplicas set to at least 1 (or more, sized to expected steady baseline traffic) so there is always a warm pool capable of serving immediately, eliminating the zero-to-one cold start entirely for normal traffic patterns.

For scale-up triggers, CPU alone is a poor proxy for a model-serving workload -- request queue depth or in-flight request count is a more direct signal of actual load and reacts faster than waiting for CPU to climb, so the scaling policy should include a custom metric (e.g. requests-in-flight or queue length) alongside or instead of CPU, with a scale-up threshold low enough to trigger before requests start queuing meaningfully. Scale-up behavior should also be tuned to add capacity aggressively (a short stabilization window, a high percentage/pod increase per scaling event) since under-provisioning during a burst directly causes the timeout problem being fixed, while scale-down should be much more conservative (a long stabilization window) to avoid flapping -- removing a replica right before the next burst arrives recreates the same cold-start cost.

For genuinely bursty or unpredictable traffic where keeping enough replicas warm at all times is too costly, the complementary pattern is a small dedicated warm pool (e.g. minReplicas sized to P50 traffic) plus pre-warming logic triggered by a leading indicator (scheduled traffic patterns, or scaling up ahead of a known event) rather than relying purely on reactive autoscaling, since reactive scaling by definition only reacts after load has already started climbing.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The root cause here is scaling to zero combined with a slow cold start -- the model has to actually load into memory before the container can serve a single request, and that's measured in tens of seconds, not milliseconds, so any request that arrives during that window just times out. CPU-based autoscaling makes it worse because while the model is loading, CPU usage doesn't necessarily look like 'scale up more' to the autoscaler -- it can look idle or spiky in a way that doesn't trigger fast enough.

The first and most impactful change I'd make is simply not scaling to zero. I'd set minReplicas to at least 1, sized to whatever the baseline traffic actually looks like, so there's always a warm, ready-to-serve replica and the zero-to-one cold start just doesn't happen for normal traffic. That alone usually kills most of the timeout problem.

Then I'd swap the scaling signal away from pure CPU utilization toward something that reflects actual request pressure -- queue depth or in-flight request count -- because that reacts to real load faster than waiting for CPU to visibly climb. And I'd deliberately make scale-up fast and aggressive -- short stabilization window, add replicas quickly -- while making scale-down slow and conservative, because the worst outcome is scaling a replica down right before the next burst hits and paying the cold-start cost all over again. If the traffic pattern is genuinely spiky and unpredictable even with a small warm pool, I'd also look at pre-warming ahead of known traffic patterns rather than relying purely on reactive scaling, since by definition reactive scaling only kicks in after the load has already started.
questions.example:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: model-server
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: model-server
  minReplicas: 2        # warm pool -- never scales to zero, avoids cold start on every burst
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric:
          name: inflight_requests_per_pod   # custom metric: queue/in-flight depth, not just CPU
        target:
          type: AverageValue
          averageValue: "5"
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0     # react immediately to bursts
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 100                    # can double capacity in one step
          periodSeconds: 30
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300   # conservative -- avoid flapping / re-triggering cold starts
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 1
          periodSeconds: 60
commonMistakes: Leaving minReplicas at 0, guaranteeing a cold start on every traffic burst after idle
Relying solely on CPU utilization as the scale-up signal for a model-serving workload
Setting symmetric scale-up/scale-down stabilization windows, causing replicas to be removed right before the next burst
Not sizing minReplicas to any real baseline traffic data, just picking an arbitrary small number
Ignoring image pull time and model-loading time entirely when reasoning about how fast a new replica can actually become useful
keyPoints: Sets minReplicas above zero to maintain a warm pool and avoid zero-to-one cold starts
Uses a request-pressure metric (queue depth/in-flight count) as a scale-up trigger, not CPU alone
Configures aggressive scale-up behavior and conservative scale-down behavior
Sizes the warm pool based on actual baseline traffic rather than an arbitrary guess
Considers pre-warming or scheduled scaling for predictable bursty traffic beyond reactive autoscaling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies scale-to-zero as the primary cause of cold-start timeouts
Sets an appropriate minReplicas warm pool
Replaces or supplements CPU-based scaling with a request-pressure metric
Configures asymmetric scale-up/scale-down behavior correctly
Valid, correct autoscaling configuration syntax

questions.title: Hallucinations After a Silent Model Upgrade
questions.prompt: Your support assistant has run reliably for six months calling the provider's API with the model alias "gpt-4-turbo" rather than a dated snapshot. Last Tuesday, with no deploy on your side, ticket volume spiked: the assistant began confidently stating a 45-day return window when the real policy is 30 days, something it had never gotten wrong before. Your eval suite still shows green because it hasn't been re-run since launch. Diagnose what most likely happened, how you'd confirm it, and how you'd fix the pipeline so it can't happen again silently.
questions.modelAnswer:
The symptom profile -- a correctness regression on a specific factual claim, with zero code or prompt changes, on a day with no deploy -- points directly at the provider moving the "gpt-4-turbo" alias to a new underlying snapshot. Aliases are intentionally mutable; the provider can repoint them to a newer checkpoint at any time, and that checkpoint can have different parametric knowledge, different instruction-following tendencies, and different hallucination patterns than the one you validated against. The deeper root cause isn't really "the model got worse," it's that the refund policy number was never grounded in the first place -- the model was answering from memorized training-adjacent text or confabulation rather than from a fact actually present in context, so any shift in the underlying weights can change what it confabulates.

To confirm, I'd check the model identifier returned in the API response metadata (most providers echo the resolved snapshot id, not just the alias you requested) and compare it against what was logged a week ago. I'd also pull the provider's model changelog/deprecation page for that date, and re-run the frozen eval set you built at launch against both the current alias and, if still available, the prior dated snapshot -- a reproducible regression on the same eval confirms the model, not a prompt or infra change, is the variable.

The fix has two parts. Immediately, pin production to a specific dated snapshot instead of a floating alias, so upgrades become an opt-in action with a changelog and a re-validation step, not a silent event. Structurally, stop letting the model answer policy facts from memory at all: inject the actual current policy text into the prompt or retrieve it from a maintained knowledge base, so the number is grounded and copy-pasted rather than generated. Finally, add a scheduled job that runs the eval suite nightly against whatever the live alias currently resolves to, so any future provider-side change is caught by an alert within a day instead of by customer complaints a week later.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd check is the model id actually returned on each call, not the alias string in our config -- if we're requesting "gpt-4-turbo" and the resolved snapshot changed between last week's logs and this week's, that's the smoking gun and I can usually find it in our own request logs without even going to the vendor. The absence of any deploy on our side is the detail that rules out everything else -- no prompt change, no retrieval change, so by elimination either the model moved or something upstream of us did.

Once I've got that confirmed, I'd go pull up the eval harness we built at launch and just rerun it as-is against production right now. If it's still green against a frozen test set, either the regression is narrower than the ticket volume suggests, or -- more likely in my experience -- our eval set never actually exercised this exact fact in the first place, which is its own finding worth fixing. I'd also replay a handful of the actual failing transcripts from support tickets to see the model's reasoning, because sometimes it'll reveal the model second-guessing itself or hedging in a way that tells you it's reaching for a fact it doesn't have.

The real fix I'd push for isn't just pinning the snapshot, though I'd do that same day as a stopgap -- it's that a policy number like a return window should never be something the model is allowed to generate from its own memory. I'd move that into context: either a short system-prompt snippet pulled from a policy doc we own, or a tiny retrieval step. That way even if the model vendor ships a new checkpoint tomorrow, the fact itself is copy-pasted, not recalled, and model drift becomes a non-event for anything that matters this much. I'd also set up a cheap nightly cron that hits the live alias with our eval set and pages us on a regression, so we're not relying on customers to be our monitoring.
questions.example: A nightly cron hitting the live alias and diffing response hashes/eval scores against yesterday's baseline would have caught the snapshot change within 24 hours instead of after a support-ticket spike.
commonMistakes: Assuming a bug in prompt code and re-reading the prompt template line by line before checking whether the model itself changed
Blaming 'random hallucination variance' and adding a retry/temperature tweak instead of identifying the upgrade
Fixing it by hardcoding the correct number into a one-off prompt patch instead of grounding the fact via retrieval or context injection
Pinning to a dated snapshot but never scheduling re-validation, so the same failure mode recurs at the next manual upgrade
Not checking the response metadata for the resolved model id, so the diagnosis stays a guess instead of a confirmed fact
keyPoints: Recognize the no-deploy, no-prompt-change signature as pointing to an external dependency change
Check response metadata / logs for the resolved model snapshot id before and after the incident
Understand that aliases are mutable and providers can repoint them without notice
Identify that the underlying problem is ungrounded factual generation, not just 'model got worse'
Propose both the immediate fix (pin snapshot) and the structural fix (ground facts via retrieval, add continuous eval monitoring)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies silent model/alias change as the likely root cause
Gives a concrete confirmation method (metadata/logs, changelog, eval rerun)
Identifies the deeper issue that the fact was ungrounded in the first place
Proposes pinning to a dated snapshot as the immediate fix
Proposes grounding via retrieval/context injection and continuous eval monitoring as the structural fix

questions.title: Intermittent Mid-Sentence Truncation in Production
questions.prompt: Your chat product is getting bug reports that roughly 2-3% of responses cut off mid-sentence, sometimes mid-word, with no error thrown on the client. It's intermittent -- the same prompt sometimes completes fine and sometimes truncates. Logs show the affected calls all complete successfully with HTTP 200. You suspect it's related to how the application sets generation limits versus how much room is left in the context window. Diagnose the root cause and describe the fix, including why it's intermittent rather than constant.
questions.modelAnswer:
A clean HTTP 200 with a truncated body is the key clue: the API call itself succeeded, which rules out network errors or timeouts, and points instead to the model hitting a hard stop condition that the application isn't surfacing. The most likely cause is that the response is being cut off by `max_tokens` (or the provider's equivalent output cap), and the reason it's intermittent rather than constant is that the amount of room left for the completion depends on how long the conversation history and retrieved context are on a given turn. On short conversations there's plenty of budget and the model finishes naturally; on longer conversations, or when a user's message triggers a long retrieved-context injection, the prompt tokens eat into a shared or capped budget and the completion gets chopped at whatever token count remains.

To confirm, I'd check the `finish_reason` field returned by the API, which most providers set to something like `"length"` when the stop is due to the token cap rather than the model naturally emitting a stop token (`"stop"`). Grep logs for `finish_reason: length` filtered to the 2-3% of affected requests, and correlate it with prompt token count on those calls -- I'd expect to see the truncated ones clustering at the longest input-token counts.

The fix has an immediate and a structural layer. Immediately, raise `max_tokens` enough to cover the actual tail of the output distribution, and instrument the app to detect `finish_reason: length` and either auto-continue the generation or retry with a larger budget rather than silently serving a chopped response. Structurally, decouple the input and output budgets explicitly -- reserve a fixed token allowance for the completion before computing how much context/history fits, rather than letting a growing prompt silently shrink the remaining room, and surface a UI-level warning or graceful "response truncated, continue?" affordance for the rare cases it still happens.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing that jumps out to me is '200 OK but truncated' -- that's not a network or infra problem, that's the model being told to stop. So my first move is to go look at `finish_reason` on the affected calls specifically, not the whole log stream, because if it says `length` instead of `stop` that basically confirms it in one line without me having to guess.

From there I'd want to understand why it's only 2-3% and not everyone, so I'd pull prompt token counts for the truncated requests versus the clean ones. My hypothesis going in is that we've got a fixed `max_tokens` setting that was sized against typical short conversations, and the long-tail users -- the ones with a long chat history or a big retrieved-context block -- are the ones whose completions get chopped, because the model simply runs out of its allotted output tokens before it's done talking. If the token counts line up with that pattern, I'm confident that's the whole story and I don't need to keep looking for something more exotic like a provider-side outage or truncated streaming.

On the fix, I'd treat this as two separate problems. The quick win is just reserving output budget properly -- decide how many tokens a complete answer realistically needs, subtract that off the top, and only let the rest of the context window be used for history and retrieval, instead of the current setup where a growing prompt silently eats into the output allowance. The more durable fix is to never let a truncated response reach the user silently in the first place -- detect `finish_reason: length` server-side and either auto-continue the generation with a follow-up call or at minimum flag it so we're not shipping half a sentence and calling it a successful 200.

questions.title: General Capability Loss After Fine-Tuning
questions.prompt: You fine-tuned a base model on 3,000 internal support tickets to make it better at classifying ticket category and tone. The fine-tuned model is indeed better at that narrow task, but QA now reports it's noticeably worse at everything else it used to handle in the same app -- it mishandles simple formatting requests, loses track of multi-turn context, and sometimes replies in an oddly clipped tone even outside the support-ticket flow. Diagnose why fine-tuning on a narrow dataset degraded general capability, and describe how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is a textbook case of catastrophic forgetting compounded by distributional overfitting. When you fine-tune on a narrow dataset -- 3,000 tickets, all support-classification in nature, likely all similarly short and similarly toned -- gradient updates push the model's weights toward minimizing loss on that distribution specifically. If training ran for several epochs with a learning rate high enough to meaningfully move the weights, the model doesn't just learn the new task, it overwrites or distorts representations that were useful for unrelated tasks (general formatting, multi-turn coherence, varied tone) that never appeared in the fine-tuning set. The 'clipped tone' leaking into unrelated flows is a strong tell: the model has partially overfit to the stylistic surface features of the ticket dataset, not just its labels.

To confirm, I'd run the pre-fine-tune base model and the fine-tuned model side by side against a general-capability eval set (not the support-ticket eval) covering formatting, multi-turn memory, and tone variety, and quantify the delta. I'd also check the training config for epoch count and learning rate -- forgetting gets worse with more epochs and higher learning rates on a small, narrow dataset.

The fix is primarily about how the tuning is done rather than whether to fine-tune at all. Switch to a parameter-efficient method like LoRA with a modest rank instead of full fine-tuning, which constrains how much the base weights can shift and preserves more general capability. Reduce epochs and use early stopping against a held-out general-capability eval, not just the task-specific validation loss. If the support-classification behavior genuinely needs to be isolated, consider routing: keep the base model for general chat and only invoke the fine-tuned (or better, a cheap classifier head) model for the specific ticket-classification subtask, so the fine-tune's narrow focus never touches unrelated traffic.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The detail that tells me this is forgetting and not just 'the model got dumber' is that the regression shows up specifically outside the fine-tuned task -- formatting, multi-turn memory, tone -- areas that were never represented in those 3,000 tickets. If I fine-tune on a narrow slice and don't actively protect the rest, the model has no reason to preserve capabilities the training data never exercised; gradient descent only cares about the loss it's being optimized against.

So the first thing I'd pull up is the training run config: how many epochs, what learning rate, full fine-tune or LoRA. My guess before even looking is that it's a full fine-tune run for multiple epochs at a learning rate tuned for fast convergence on the narrow task, which is exactly the recipe for overwriting broader representations. I'd validate that by running the base model and the tuned model against a general-purpose eval set side by side -- if the base model handles multi-turn and formatting fine and the tuned one doesn't, that's the fingerprint of forgetting, not a dataset-labeling problem.

For the fix, I'd push back on full fine-tuning for this use case entirely. A narrow classification-style task on 3,000 examples is almost always better served by LoRA or another adapter method with constrained rank, which limits how much the underlying weights can move, plus fewer epochs and early stopping checked against the general eval, not just the task-specific validation loss. And honestly, if the only goal is categorizing ticket type and tone, I'd seriously consider whether we need to fine-tune the whole conversational model at all versus training a small, separate classifier and keeping the general-purpose model untouched for everything else -- that way a narrow optimization target can never bleed into unrelated behavior.
questions.example: Running the same 20-prompt general-capability eval (multi-turn recall, formatting instructions, tone variety) against both the base and fine-tuned checkpoints and seeing the fine-tuned model drop from 95% to 60% pass rate confirms forgetting rather than a fluke.

Adding more fine-tuning data on the same narrow task, which worsens forgetting instead of fixing it

Jumping straight to 'rewrite the system prompt' to compensate for tone drift instead of addressing the underlying weight shift
Using full fine-tuning by default without considering LoRA/adapters or reduced epochs for a small, narrow dataset

questions.title: LLM Cost Tripled Overnight With No Usage Spike
questions.prompt: Your finance team flags that yesterday's LLM API bill was triple the daily average, but your dashboard shows request volume (unique user sessions) was flat, even slightly down. Nothing in your deployment calendar shows a release yesterday. You pull the provider's usage breakdown and notice token consumption per request is up roughly 4x while request count matches historical norms. Diagnose the likely cause(s) and describe how you'd confirm which one it is and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Flat request count with 4x token consumption per request means the cost increase is coming from what each call is doing, not how often it's called -- so the investigation should focus on per-call token accounting rather than traffic. There are three usual suspects: a retry loop silently re-sending the same expensive call multiple times on transient errors, a change in retrieved context size (e.g. a RAG pipeline suddenly pulling more or larger chunks), or a model/parameter change that increased output length or switched to a pricier model tier, possibly via an automatic routing/fallback path triggered by rate limits or errors upstream.

To isolate which one, I'd pull a sample of yesterday's request logs and look at the breakdown between prompt tokens and completion tokens specifically, plus a count of calls per logical user action -- if a single user action is generating multiple API calls where it used to generate one, that's the retry/loop signature. If prompt tokens specifically ballooned, that points to context/retrieval bloat. If completion tokens ballooned with prompt tokens flat, that points to an output-length or model-tier change, which I'd confirm by checking the model id field in logs for an unexpected fallback model.

Once isolated, the fix follows directly: cap and alert on retry counts per logical request and fix whatever upstream condition (rate limit, transient 5xx) is triggering the retries; audit the retrieval step for a recent change in chunk count/size or a broken deduplication step feeding duplicate context; and if it's a routing/fallback issue, pin the model explicitly and alert on any fallback activation rather than letting it silently route to a more expensive model. In all cases, add a per-request token budget alert so a 4x spike triggers a page the same day, not after the monthly bill lands.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start exactly where the data already points me -- request count is flat, tokens-per-request is 4x, so this isn't a traffic problem, it's a 'what is each call actually doing' problem. I wouldn't waste time looking at session dashboards again; I'd go straight to the token accounting in the provider logs.

My mental checklist for what causes tokens-per-request to balloon without more requests is pretty short: either we're calling the API more times per user action than we think (a retry loop hiding behind what looks like 'one request' at the product level), we're sending more context per call (a RAG or memory change inflating the prompt), or we're generating longer or pricier completions per call (an output-length regression or a silent fallback to a bigger model). So I'd split prompt tokens from completion tokens in yesterday's logs first, because that one split tells me which of those three buckets to chase -- prompt tokens up means context bloat, completion tokens up means generation/model-tier, and if both look normal per call but call-count-per-action is up, that's the retry loop.

Once I know which bucket, the fix is usually mechanical: if it's retries, find the upstream error causing them and add a hard cap with backoff and an alert instead of silent unlimited retries; if it's context bloat, check whatever changed in the retrieval or memory logic recently -- even an unrelated deploy to a shared service can change chunk sizes; if it's model routing, pin the model explicitly and treat any fallback to a different model as a paged incident, not a silent default. And regardless of root cause, I'd walk away from this making sure we have a same-day alert on token-per-request anomalies so finance isn't the ones discovering a 3x cost spike a month later.
questions.example: Splitting yesterday's token logs into prompt_tokens vs completion_tokens per call and finding completion_tokens jumped from an average of 300 to 1,400 while prompt_tokens stayed flat points straight at an output-length or model-tier change rather than retries or context bloat.

Assuming it's a provider pricing change without checking the account's own usage breakdown first
Fixing it by just setting a budget cap/kill switch without identifying which of retries, context bloat, or model routing caused it
Not splitting prompt vs completion tokens, so the diagnosis stays vague ('tokens are up') instead of actionable
Overlooking that an unrelated deploy to a shared retrieval/memory service could be the true cause, since 'no deploy in our calendar' only covers the immediate app

questions.title: Multimodal Feature Fails Silently on Real User Images
questions.prompt: A vision-language feature that extracts data from photos of receipts passed all 200 test images with over 95% field-extraction accuracy. In production, though, support is seeing a cluster of complaints where the model returns plausible-looking but wrong totals, or silently omits line items, specifically for photos taken at an angle, in low light, or as very large (12MP+) phone camera files. The model doesn't error out -- it just returns incorrect structured output with normal-looking confidence language. Diagnose why production images are failing differently from the test set, and describe your fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
The core problem is a mismatch between the test set's image distribution and production's: the 200 test images were almost certainly clean, well-lit, roughly front-facing scans or photos, while production images reflect real phone-camera conditions -- skew, glare, low light, and very large raw resolutions. Two distinct failure modes are likely compounding. First, large images get resized or compressed by the preprocessing pipeline (or by the provider's own input handling) down to a token-budget-friendly size, and if that resizing is naive (simple downscale without contrast/sharpness correction) it can blur small receipt text below legibility while still looking fine at a glance. Second, angled or low-light photos stress the model's OCR-like capability in a way clean scans never do, and critically, the model isn't trained to say 'I can't read this' -- it's trained to produce a plausible structured output regardless, so it fills in a reasonable-looking total or drops a line it couldn't parse, with no drop in stated confidence because the model has no real confidence signal to report.

To confirm, I'd pull the actual failing production images and run them back through the pipeline with and without the app's own preprocessing step, and separately through the raw model at full resolution, to see where the information loss happens -- preprocessing resize versus genuine model limitation at that angle/lighting.

The fix starts with the test set itself: it needs to be rebuilt to include angled, low-light, and high-resolution real-world photos, not just clean scans, so this failure mode would have been caught before launch. On the pipeline side, add an image-quality gate before the model call -- checking resolution, blur, and basic brightness heuristics -- and either prompt the user to retake the photo or apply targeted preprocessing (deskew, contrast normalization, smart downscaling that preserves text sharpness) when quality is borderline. Finally, since the model has no reliable self-reported confidence, add a cross-check: validate extracted totals against line-item sums, and flag or request confirmation when they don't reconcile, rather than trusting the model's structured output blindly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The gap that jumps out at me immediately is '95% on 200 test images' versus real complaints clustering on angled, low-light, high-res photos -- that's not a flaky model, that's a test set that never exercised the conditions production actually has. Phone photos of receipts are messy by default; a curated test set of clean scans was always going to look great and tell us almost nothing about this.

So my first move would be to go grab the actual complaint images, not synthetic ones, and run them through the pipeline step by step -- what does the image look like right before it hits the model, after whatever resizing or compression our preprocessing does. My suspicion is we'll find the 12MP images are getting aggressively downscaled to fit a token budget, and that downscaling is probably naive, so fine print on a receipt turns to mush before the model even sees it. For the angled and low-light ones, I'd expect that's more of a genuine model limitation, and the thing to internalize there is that these models don't have a reliable 'I'm not sure' signal -- they're going to emit a confident-looking total whether they actually read it correctly or guessed, so we can't lean on the model's own tone to catch its mistakes.

Given that, I'd fix this in layers. First, rebuild the eval set with real-world messy photos so we'd actually catch this kind of regression next time, because a clean 95% number was giving us false confidence. Second, add a quality gate before the model call -- cheap heuristics for blur, brightness, and resolution -- and either preprocess intelligently (deskew, contrast fix, smarter downscaling) or just ask the user to retake the photo when it's clearly too degraded. And third, since I can't trust the model to flag its own uncertainty, I'd add a deterministic sanity check after extraction -- do the line items actually sum to the stated total -- and treat a mismatch as a signal to flag the result for review rather than serving it as-is.
questions.example: Running a failing 12MP low-light photo through the pipeline shows it gets downscaled from 4000x3000 to 768x576 before reaching the model -- at that resolution the receipt's smallest line-item text is only a few pixels tall, which explains the silently dropped items.
