Trying to fix it by switching to a 'better' vision model without addressing the preprocessing/downscaling step
Trusting the model's confident tone as a proxy for correctness, since these models don't reliably signal uncertainty
Not adding any deterministic validation (e.g. line-item sum reconciliation) to catch wrong structured output after the fact

questions.title: Prompt Works in Testing, Fails on Real Users' Long Inputs
questions.prompt: A prompt template that performed well in QA -- where test inputs averaged 200 words -- starts ignoring its system instructions once it ships, specifically for the subset of real users who paste in long documents (sometimes 3,000+ words) for summarization. The model stops respecting the output format instructions and occasionally stops respecting a safety instruction that was supposed to prevent it from giving financial advice. Diagnose the root cause and describe your fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is a context-budget and instruction-placement failure that only manifests at input lengths QA never tested. If the system prompt and formatting/safety instructions are placed before the user's content, and the application has any kind of token-budget trimming logic (either explicit truncation to fit a context limit, or the model's own tendency to under-weight instructions that are far from the content it's actively generating from), then a 200-word test input leaves plenty of 'attention budget' for the instructions to dominate, while a 3,000-word document pushes the instructions further from the generation point in relative terms and gives the model far more competing content to attend to. If there's an explicit truncation step in the pipeline, it's also worth checking whether it ever truncates from the front of the prompt (where the system instructions live) rather than the back, which would literally delete the instructions rather than just diluting their influence.

To confirm, I'd log the exact assembled prompt (system instructions plus user content) for both a passing short-input case and a failing long-input case, check the total token count against the model's context limit, and verify whether any instructions were truncated outright versus just diluted. I'd also test the same long document with instructions moved to directly before and after the content to see if placement alone changes the failure rate.

The fix is to treat instruction adherence as a token-budget design problem, not just a wording problem. Reserve a fixed budget for the system/safety instructions and never let user content truncation eat into them. Repeat critical instructions (format and safety) both before and after the long user content, since models tend to weight instructions near the end of the prompt more heavily, and consider summarizing or chunking very long documents before the final instruction-following pass so the instruction-to-content ratio stays closer to what was validated in testing. Finally, expand the QA input-length distribution to include realistic long documents so this gets caught before shipping next time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The tell here is that it's specifically the long-input users who are affected, and QA's average input was 200 words -- so whatever's breaking only shows up once the prompt gets big, and that's almost always a context-budget or instruction-placement issue, not a wording problem with the instructions themselves.

First thing I'd do is log the full assembled prompt for one of the failing long-document cases and actually read it end to end, token count included. I'm checking two things: is anything getting truncated outright -- because if there's a trimming step and it's cutting from the front, it might literally be deleting the system instructions on long inputs -- and if nothing's being truncated, where do the instructions sit relative to the 3,000 words of content. My bet is the instructions are up front, and once there's that much user content between them and the point where the model starts generating, the model's attention just doesn't weight them as strongly anymore, even though technically every token is still there.

To fix it, I wouldn't just rewrie the instructions and hope -- I'd restructure where they live in the prompt. Repeating the key instructions, especially the safety one around financial advice, right before the generation point as well as at the top gives the model a much stronger signal on long inputs. I'd also make sure our token-budget trimming, if we have any, is explicitly protecting the instruction tokens and never eating into them regardless of how long the user content gets. And separately, I'd flag to the team that QA's test corpus needs real long-document examples in it, because a 200-word average completely missed this failure mode, and it'll miss the next one too if we don't fix the test distribution.
questions.example: Moving the format and safety instructions to appear both before and after a 3,000-word document (instead of only before it) raised instruction-adherence from roughly 60% to over 95% on a sample of long-document test cases.

questions.title: Chain-of-Thought Adds Cost Without Adding Accuracy
questions.prompt: A teammate added "think step by step before answering" to the prompt for a sentiment-tagging task (classify customer messages as positive, negative, or neutral) because it helped on a harder reasoning task elsewhere in the product. On this task, it increased average latency from 400ms to 2.1 seconds and roughly tripled token cost per call, but accuracy on your labeled eval set only moved from 91.2% to 91.6% -- within noise. Diagnose why chain-of-thought isn't paying off here, and recommend what to do instead.
questions.modelAnswer:
Chain-of-thought helps most on tasks that genuinely require multi-step reasoning -- arithmetic, multi-hop logic, planning -- where the model benefits from externalizing intermediate steps before committing to an answer. Sentiment tagging of short customer messages is close to the opposite: it's a largely pattern-matching classification task where a capable model can usually map surface features (word choice, punctuation, tone markers) directly to a label without needing an intermediate reasoning chain. Forcing CoT on a task that doesn't need it doesn't just add unnecessary tokens; it can occasionally introduce noise by giving the model room to talk itself into an overthought or second-guessed answer on genuinely ambiguous short messages, which is consistent with the accuracy gain being within noise rather than a real improvement.

To confirm, I'd look at where the few percentage points of difference actually occur -- if the CoT version's wins and losses are roughly symmetric and concentrated on the same ambiguous messages (sarcasm, mixed sentiment) rather than showing a clear net improvement, that supports 'no real reasoning benefit, just noise.' I'd also inspect a sample of the generated reasoning chains; if they just restate the message and assert a label without doing any real multi-step inference, that's further evidence the task doesn't need the structure CoT provides.

The recommendation is to drop CoT for this task and instead invest the saved latency/cost budget into things that actually move classification accuracy: better few-shot examples covering the genuinely hard cases (sarcasm, mixed sentiment, negation), a slightly larger or better-suited base model if budget allows, or calibration/confidence thresholding with human review for low-confidence cases. If a harder subset of this task does benefit from reasoning (e.g. multi-sentence messages with conflicting sentiment), consider routing only that subset through a CoT-enabled path rather than applying it uniformly to every call.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first question I'd ask is whether this task actually needs reasoning at all, because chain-of-thought's whole value proposition is helping the model work through multiple steps before committing -- and classifying a short customer message as positive, negative, or neutral is mostly pattern recognition, not multi-step logic. So before even looking at the numbers, my prior is that CoT was probably never going to help much here; it got added because it worked elsewhere, which is a classic case of a technique getting over-applied past the problem it actually solves.

The numbers back that up for me -- a 0.4 point accuracy move against a 5x latency increase and 3x cost is well within what I'd call noise for a binary-ish classification eval, not a real signal. What I'd actually want to look at is the generated reasoning text itself on a sample of calls. If I read through those chains and they're basically just restating the message and then asserting a label, that confirms the model isn't doing anything with that extra generation that it couldn't do directly -- it's just verbalizing a decision it already made.

Given that, I'd recommend pulling CoT off this task and redirecting the effort somewhere it'll actually move the number -- better few-shot examples targeting the genuinely hard cases like sarcasm or mixed sentiment, or tightening up the label definitions if there's ambiguity in how 'neutral' versus 'negative' gets decided at the edges. If there's a real subset of messages that's legitimately hard -- long, multi-clause, conflicting sentiment -- I'd consider a cheap router that sends only that slice through a reasoning-enabled path, rather than paying the 5x latency tax on every single simple message to maybe help a handful of edge cases.

questions.title: A Small Prompt Tweak Caused a Silent Downstream Regression
questions.prompt: A teammate shipped what looked like a harmless prompt tweak: rewording an instruction from "Summarize the ticket" to "Briefly summarize the ticket" to reduce verbosity. Two weeks later, a different team discovers that a downstream automation relying on the summary's structure (it parses out a specific "Action items:" section) has been silently failing for half those two weeks, because the shorter summaries frequently drop that section entirely. No alerts fired and no one noticed until a customer complained that their follow-up task never got created. Diagnose the process failure here (not just the prompt's wording) and propose a fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
The prompt wording itself is almost a side detail here; the real failure is organizational and process-level: there was no automated eval gate that would have caught this regression before it shipped, and no monitoring that would have caught it in the two weeks it was live in production. 'Briefly summarize' is a reasonable instruction in isolation, but it directly conflicts with an implicit downstream contract -- that the summary always includes an 'Action items:' section -- that was never encoded anywhere the prompt author could see it. Prompts in production systems are effectively APIs with consumers, but unlike a typical API change, there was no schema, no contract test, and no changelog connecting the prompt to the thing depending on its output structure.

To confirm this is a process gap rather than a one-off fluke, I'd check whether there's any existing regression eval set at all for this prompt, and if there is, whether it includes a check for the presence of the 'Action items:' section specifically -- if it doesn't, that's the direct cause. I'd also check whether there's any output-schema validation on the consuming side (the automation that parses the section) -- if that parser fails closed and silently on a missing section rather than raising an alert, that's a second, independent gap that let the failure run for two weeks undetected.

The fix has three layers. First, immediately revert or adjust the prompt to explicitly require the 'Action items:' section regardless of brevity. Second, build a regression eval set for this prompt that encodes the real downstream contract as an automated check (e.g. 'output must contain an Action items: section when the ticket has follow-up tasks'), and gate any prompt change on that eval passing in CI before merge. Third, fix the blast-radius problem: the consuming automation should validate the structure of what it parses and alert loudly on a parse failure rather than silently doing nothing, so that even a future, different regression is caught within hours, not weeks.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Honestly the wording change itself barely matters to me -- 'briefly summarize' is a perfectly reasonable thing to want. What actually went wrong is that nobody had a safety net that would catch a behavior change before it reached a system that depended on very specific output structure. So I'd frame this as two separate process gaps, not one prompt bug.

Gap one: was there any automated eval running against this prompt before merge? If there wasn't, or if there was but it never checked for the 'Action items:' section specifically, then there was no way this regression could have been caught pre-ship, no matter how careful the person making the wording tweak was -- they had no way of knowing a downstream team's automation depended on that exact section existing. That's not really their fault; that's a missing contract.

Gap two, and this is the one that bugs me more: it ran silently in production for two weeks. That means whatever's parsing out 'Action items:' on the consuming side is failing closed -- no section found, no alert, just quietly not creating the follow-up task. I'd want that parser to be loud about a missing expected section, because a silent failure mode like that will keep biting us on completely different prompts in the future if we don't fix it at the consumption layer too.

So my fix is really about building the missing scaffolding: a regression eval set for this prompt that encodes the real contract -- 'if the ticket has follow-up items, the output must contain an Action items section' -- wired into CI so no prompt change merges without passing it, and a loud failure/alert on the consuming side whenever the expected structure isn't found. That combination means next time someone makes an innocuous-looking wording tweak, either the eval catches it in minutes, or if it somehow slips through, the downstream alert catches it in hours instead of two weeks.

questions.title: Retrieval Looks Right, the Answer Still Isn't
questions.prompt: You're debugging a RAG-based internal Q&A tool. For a specific failing query, you check the retrieval logs and confirm the top-3 retrieved chunks are exactly the right ones -- they contain the correct, unambiguous answer in plain text. Yet the model's final answer is wrong, stating something that directly contradicts what's in the retrieved context. This happens on roughly 8% of queries where retrieval is independently verified as correct. Diagnose why the generation step is failing even with correct context, and describe your fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
When retrieval is confirmed correct but the final answer contradicts it, the failure has moved from a retrieval problem to a faithfulness problem -- the model is generating an answer that isn't actually grounded in the provided context, despite the context being right there. A few concrete mechanisms commonly cause this: the correct chunk may be present but buried in the middle or end of a longer context block where models are known to pay less attention (the 'lost in the middle' effect), the prompt may not explicitly instruct the model to prioritize the provided context over its own prior knowledge when the two conflict, or the retrieved chunk may contain the right answer alongside other, superficially similar but incorrect information that the model latches onto instead.

To confirm which mechanism is at play, I'd inspect the exact assembled prompt for several of the 8% failing cases: where in the context block does the correct chunk sit relative to other chunks, does the system prompt explicitly instruct 'answer only using the provided context, and if the context conflicts with what you know, trust the context,' and does the chunk contain any adjacent text that could plausibly be confused with the answer. I'd also check whether failures correlate with position (chunk ranked 2nd or 3rd rather than 1st) or with the presence of similar-but-wrong facts nearby.

The fix layers: add an explicit faithfulness instruction to the prompt that tells the model to ground its answer strictly in the provided context and to say so if the context doesn't contain the answer. Reorder context so the highest-relevance chunk appears last, right before the question, since recency within the prompt tends to get more attention than middle position. For queries where this matters most, add a verification/faithfulness check as a second pass -- have the model (or a smaller/cheaper checker) confirm the answer is actually supported by the cited context before returning it, and regenerate or flag for review if it isn't.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing that reframes this problem for me immediately is 'retrieval is confirmed correct.' That rules out the usual first suspects -- bad embeddings, wrong chunking, bad similarity search -- and tells me the bug lives entirely in generation: the model has the right information in front of it and still produces a wrong answer. That's a faithfulness problem, which is a different debugging path than a retrieval problem.

So I'd go look at the exact prompt that got sent for a handful of these 8% failures, specifically two things: where does the correct chunk sit in the context block, and does the system prompt say anything at all about how to treat the provided context relative to what the model might already 'know.' My experience is that a lot of RAG prompts just dump the retrieved chunks in with something generic like 'use the following context to answer,' with no explicit instruction about precedence when the model's own prior knowledge disagrees with the context -- and models will sometimes default to their parametric knowledge, especially if the correct chunk isn't the first one they read.

On the fix side, there are really two independent levers. One is prompt-level: be explicit that the model must answer strictly from the provided context and say so when it can't, and put the most relevant chunk last, closest to the question, since models tend to weight recent context more heavily than something buried in the middle. The other lever is architectural: for a tool like this where wrong answers are costly, I'd add a cheap faithfulness check as a second step -- literally ask the model, or a smaller one, 'does this answer follow from this context, yes or no' -- and either regenerate or flag for human review on a 'no.' That turns an invisible 8% silent failure rate into something that gets caught before the user sees it.
questions.example: Re-running a failing query with the correct chunk moved to the last position in the context block and an added instruction to 'answer only from the provided context' flips the output from the wrong contradicted answer to the correct one, confirming it was a faithfulness/attention issue rather than a retrieval issue.

Assuming the model is simply 'unreliable' without checking context ordering or explicit faithfulness instructions
Fixing it by retrieving more chunks (increasing k) when the real chunk was already present and correct
Not inspecting the exact assembled prompt, so the diagnosis stays speculative instead of confirmed
Not adding any post-hoc faithfulness verification, leaving the same 8% failure rate as a permanent silent risk

questions.title: Retrieval Quality Collapses After an Embedding Model Upgrade
questions.prompt: Your team upgraded the embedding model used for your RAG pipeline's vector search, expecting better retrieval quality based on its benchmark scores. Instead, retrieval relevance dropped sharply in production -- the top-k results for common queries are now often unrelated to the query. The vector database itself wasn't touched, and the new embedding model is confirmed to be working correctly when tested standalone. Diagnose what went wrong and describe the fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is almost certainly a stale-index problem: the existing vector store still holds embeddings generated by the old model, but queries are now being embedded with the new model before being compared against those old vectors. Different embedding models produce vectors in entirely different, mutually incompatible geometric spaces -- even if both are high quality individually, a vector from model A and a vector from model B have no meaningful distance relationship to each other, so cosine similarity or dot-product search between a new-model query vector and old-model document vectors is essentially comparing two different coordinate systems and will return near-random results for anything beyond coincidental overlap. The fact that the new model tests fine standalone but fails in the full pipeline is the key diagnostic signal -- the model is correct, the index it's being compared against is not.

To confirm, I'd embed a known document with both the old and new model and check whether the new model's query embeddings land anywhere near the new model's embedding of that same document versus the old model's stored vector for it -- they won't be comparably close, confirming a cross-model mismatch rather than a quality regression in the new model itself.

The fix is a full re-index: re-embed every document in the corpus with the new model and rebuild the vector index from scratch before cutting query traffic over to it. Depending on corpus size, this can be done as a blue-green migration -- build the new index fully in parallel, validate retrieval quality against it with a held-out eval set, and only switch query traffic once it's confirmed healthy, rather than upgrading the embedding model and the live index at the same moment. Going forward, treat embedding model version as part of the index's identity (e.g. version-tag the index), so any future embedding model change is forced through a re-index step rather than being possible to deploy independently.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The detail that makes this easy to diagnose is 'the new model works fine standalone.' That immediately tells me the model itself isn't the problem -- it's a mismatch between the model and whatever it's being compared against. And the only thing on the other side of a similarity search is the vector index, which we're told wasn't touched. Put those two together and the answer is almost definitely a stale index: we swapped the thing that embeds queries but never re-embedded the documents that are already sitting in the database.

I'd confirm this pretty quickly by taking one document I know should rank highly for some query, embedding that same document fresh with the new model, and comparing that against what's actually stored in the index for that document. If they're meaningfully different vectors -- and they will be, because different embedding models don't share a coordinate space -- that's the whole story right there. Comparing a new-model query vector against an old-model document vector isn't really 'degraded similarity,' it's closer to comparing apples to a completely different fruit; any relevance that survives is basically coincidence.

So the fix isn't a tuning problem, it's an operational one: re-embed the entire corpus with the new model and rebuild the index before sending any query traffic to it. I'd do that as a parallel build rather than an in-place swap -- stand up the new index fully, run our retrieval eval set against it to confirm quality actually improved the way the benchmarks promised, and only then cut traffic over. And I'd make sure we don't repeat this: the embedding model version should be treated as part of what defines an index, so changing one always forces a rebuild of the other instead of being something that can quietly drift apart.
questions.example: Comparing the stored vector for a known document against a freshly computed embedding of that same document using the new model shows near-zero cosine similarity between the two, confirming the index still holds old-model vectors being queried with new-model embeddings.

Tuning top-k or similarity thresholds to compensate, which can't fix a fundamental cross-model vector mismatch
Re-testing the embedding model in isolation repeatedly without checking whether the index itself was re-embedded
Performing an in-place model swap on live query traffic without first validating a freshly rebuilt index offline
Not treating embedding model version as part of the index's identity, risking the same mismatch on a future upgrade

Identify the stale index (old-model vectors being queried by new-model embeddings) as the root cause
Propose a concrete confirmation method comparing fresh vs stored embeddings for a known document
Propose a full re-index/re-embedding of the corpus as the required fix
Recommend a blue-green/parallel-build migration pattern with validation before cutting over traffic

questions.title: Vector Search Latency Creeping Up as the Corpus Grows
questions.prompt: Your vector database powered fast retrieval (p95 under 80ms) when the corpus had 200,000 documents. Over the past year it's grown to 4 million documents with no index configuration changes, and p95 query latency has crept up to 900ms, with occasional spikes over 2 seconds under concurrent load. No code changes were made to the retrieval path. Diagnose why latency degraded and describe how you'd fix it, including tradeoffs of your recommended approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
A 20x corpus growth with zero configuration changes is a classic case of an index that was fine at small scale hitting the scaling wall of its underlying algorithm and infrastructure. If the index is using an exact or brute-force nearest-neighbor search (common as a default or for small datasets), query cost grows roughly linearly with corpus size, so a 20x increase in documents would plausibly explain something in the ballpark of a 10-20x latency increase on its own. Even with an approximate nearest-neighbor index like HNSW or IVF, default parameters tuned implicitly for a 200K-document corpus (e.g. graph connectivity or number of IVF partitions) become suboptimal at 4 million documents, and the index may also now exceed available memory, forcing disk access or eviction that wasn't happening before. The additional spikes under concurrent load point to resource contention (CPU or memory pressure) compounding the base latency increase.

To confirm, I'd check what index type and parameters are actually configured, check memory usage/eviction metrics on the vector database host, and benchmark query latency against corpus size directly (e.g. by querying a 200K-document snapshot of the current data versus the full 4M) to isolate how much of the regression is pure scale versus a separate infra issue like memory pressure.

The fix depends on what's found, but the general path is to move to or re-tune an approximate nearest-neighbor index appropriate for the new scale (e.g. increasing HNSW's M/ef parameters or IVF's partition count, or switching from exact search to ANN if that wasn't already in place), ensure the index and its working set fit in available memory (scaling the instance or sharding the index across nodes), and add metadata pre-filtering where applicable so searches operate over a narrower relevant subset rather than the full 4 million vectors. The tradeoff with ANN tuning is always recall versus latency -- more aggressive approximation reduces latency but can let relevant documents be missed, so any parameter change should be validated against a retrieval-quality eval set, not just a latency benchmark, before rolling out.
questions.professionalAnswer:
A 20x growth in corpus size with latency going from 80ms to 900ms, with zero code changes, tells me this is almost certainly a scaling problem with the index itself rather than a bug anyone introduced. My first question is simply: what kind of index are we running, and what were its parameters tuned for? If it's exact nearest-neighbor search, scaling close to linearly with data size is expected behavior, not a mystery -- the question becomes why we never put an approximate index in front of it. If it's already an ANN index like HNSW or IVF, then the likely story is its parameters were implicitly sized for 200K documents and nobody revisited them as the corpus grew 20x.

Before proposing a fix, I'd want to isolate how much of this is pure algorithmic scaling versus an infra problem layered on top, because the latency spikes under concurrent load smell like memory pressure to me -- if the index no longer comfortably fits in RAM at 4 million vectors, you'd see exactly this pattern: elevated baseline latency from disk access, with spikes under load as multiple queries contend for the same scarce memory. I'd check memory and eviction metrics on the vector DB host directly to confirm or rule that out.

Once I know which it is, the fix is usually some combination of re-tuning or introducing a proper ANN index sized for the current scale, making sure the index's working set actually fits in memory -- scaling the instance or sharding across nodes if it doesn't -- and adding metadata filtering upstream of the vector search wherever queries have a natural narrowing dimension, so we're not doing a full nearest-neighbor search over 4 million vectors when the answer could be found in a relevant 50,000-document slice. The one thing I'd flag as a real tradeoff, and test for before shipping: tightening ANN parameters for speed trades off recall, so I wouldn't roll out a latency fix without re-running it against our retrieval-quality eval set to make sure we haven't quietly started missing relevant documents to save milliseconds.
questions.example: Benchmarking the same query against a 200K-document snapshot and the full 4M-document index and finding the 200K case still returns in ~80ms confirms the degradation scales with corpus size rather than being caused by an unrelated infra regression.

Jumping straight to 'add more hardware' without first identifying whether the index type/parameters are the actual bottleneck
Tuning ANN parameters purely for lower latency without re-validating retrieval quality/recall against an eval set
Not checking whether the index and its working set still fit in available memory as the corpus grew
Ignoring the concurrent-load spike detail, which points to resource contention rather than pure per-query algorithmic cost

Distinguish exact vs approximate nearest-neighbor search and their different scaling behavior
Identify memory pressure/eviction as a likely contributor to both baseline latency and concurrent-load spikes

Explicitly name the recall-vs-latency tradeoff and the need to validate against a retrieval-quality eval set

questions.title: The RAG Assistant Cites a Source That Doesn't Support Its Answer
questions.prompt: Users of your internal RAG-based policy assistant report that it often cites a specific document (e.g. "Per Section 4.2 of the Expense Policy...") with total confidence, but when they open that section themselves, it says nothing related to the claim, or sometimes contradicts it. The correct supporting information, when it exists at all, is often in a completely different document. This erodes trust badly since it looks authoritative. Diagnose the citation/attribution failure mode and describe your fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is a specific and dangerous failure mode: citation hallucination, where the model generates a plausible-sounding answer and then separately generates a plausible-sounding citation to go with it, without the citation actually being mechanically tied to the retrieved content that informed (or didn't inform) the answer. It happens because most naive RAG implementations ask the model to both answer the question and name its source in the same free-form generation step, and the model is just as capable of confabulating a specific-sounding section number as it is of confabulating a fact -- a confident citation format ('Section 4.2') makes the hallucination look more credible, not less likely. This is often worse when the actual retrieved context doesn't contain a good answer at all; rather than saying so, the model produces an answer from general knowledge or pattern completion and then invents a citation that matches the house style of real ones.

To confirm, I'd take several of the failing examples and check whether the retrieved chunks for that query actually included the cited document/section at all -- if the cited section wasn't even among the chunks sent to the model, that proves the citation is fabricated rather than mis-cited, which is the more common and worse version of this bug.

The fix is to stop asking the model to generate citations freely and instead make citation a mechanical, structural property of the pipeline rather than a generated one. Tag each retrieved chunk with its real source and section identifier, require the model's answer to reference chunks by an index or id you control (e.g. '[doc_3]'), and then programmatically map that id back to the real source metadata to render the citation -- so the citation is always accurate by construction because it's not something the model is free to invent. Separately, add a faithfulness check that flags or blocks answers that aren't actually grounded in the chunks that were retrieved, and have the assistant explicitly say 'I couldn't find this in the available policy documents' when the retrieved context doesn't support an answer, rather than producing a confident, well-formatted guess.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This one's a specific pattern I've seen before: the model isn't failing to answer and failing to cite as two separate problems -- it's generating both the answer and a citation to go with it in the same breath, and it's just as willing to make up a believable-looking section number as it is to make up a fact. A confident-sounding citation actually makes this worse for trust, because it looks like evidence when it's really just the model matching the style of a real citation.

To confirm that's what's happening rather than a retrieval mis-rank, I'd pick a few bad examples and check what chunks were actually retrieved and sent to the model for that query. My strong suspicion is that in a good chunk of these, the cited section wasn't even in the retrieved context at all -- the model wasn't quoting a wrong source, it fabricated a plausible one out of thin air because nothing in its context told it what the real source was.

The structural fix I'd push for is to take citation generation away from the model entirely. Instead of letting it write 'Per Section 4.2,' have the retrieval step tag every chunk with an id tied to its real source and section, have the model reference answers by that id, and then do the actual citation rendering ourselves by looking up what that id really maps to. That way a citation can never be wrong, because it was never something the model was allowed to invent in the first place -- it's a lookup, not a generation. On top of that, I'd want an explicit 'I don't have this in the available documents' fallback path for when retrieval genuinely comes up empty, because right now the model's only options are 'answer confidently' or 'answer confidently with a fabricated citation,' and neither of those is acceptable for a policy assistant people are trusting at face value.
questions.example: Checking the retrieved chunks for a failing query and finding that 'Section 4.2' never appears among them -- only Sections 2.1 and 3.4 were retrieved -- confirms the citation was fabricated rather than simply misattributed.

Not implementing structural/mechanical citation (id-based lookup tied to real metadata), relying instead on the model to generate citation text freely
Not adding an explicit 'not found in available documents' fallback, so the model's only options remain confident answer or confident fabrication

questions.title: An Agent Stuck in a Tool-Calling Loop That Never Terminates
questions.prompt: An autonomous agent tasked with reconciling a customer's order history calls a `search_orders` tool, then calls it again with slightly different search parameters, then again, repeating this with minor argument variations for over 40 calls before hitting a hard timeout, never producing a final answer. The tool itself returns valid results each time; it's not erroring. This has happened on roughly 5% of reconciliation tasks since the agent was given a second, similar tool (`search_orders_by_date`) last week. Diagnose the root cause and describe your fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
The timing detail -- this started after a second, overlapping tool was added -- is the central clue. When an agent has two tools whose purposes genuinely overlap (`search_orders` and `search_orders_by_date` likely both return order data, just filterable differently), the agent has no strong signal for which one is correct for a given sub-goal, and if neither call returns a result that satisfies whatever internal termination condition the agent is checking for (e.g. 'found the exact order matching all criteria'), it will keep trying variations -- different tool, different parameters, different phrasing -- because from its perspective the task isn't done, not because it's confused in an obviously broken way. This is compounded if there's no explicit max-iteration or max-tool-call limit, and no step where the agent is prompted to recognize 'I've tried N approaches and none are converging, I should stop and report partial results or ask for help' rather than just trying the next variation indefinitely.

To confirm, I'd replay the transcript of a failing run and check two things: whether the tool descriptions for the two search tools are ambiguous enough that the agent can't cleanly decide which applies, and whether the agent's loop ever considers stopping, or whether it's architecturally just 'call a tool, evaluate, call another tool' with no exit condition besides eventually finding a satisfying result or hitting the hard timeout.

The fix operates on three levels. First, fix the tool-selection ambiguity directly: tighten the tool descriptions to make their distinct use cases unambiguous (e.g. 'use search_orders_by_date only when the user specifies a date range; otherwise use search_orders'), which is the most direct fix for a routing problem introduced by adding an overlapping tool. Second, add a hard action/iteration limit well below the timeout (e.g. 8-10 tool calls) so a confused agent fails fast and visibly rather than burning 40 calls and a timeout. Third, add an explicit reflection step after some number of unsuccessful attempts that forces the agent to either try a genuinely different strategy, return a best-effort partial answer, or escalate to a human, instead of looping on minor variations of the same approach indefinitely.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The fact that this started right after a second overlapping tool got added is basically the whole diagnosis for me before I even look at a transcript. Two tools that both search orders, just sliced differently, is exactly the kind of thing that confuses an agent's routing logic -- it's not that the agent is broken, it's that from the model's perspective neither tool call is cleanly 'wrong,' so if the result doesn't satisfy whatever condition it's internally chasing, trying the other tool, or the same tool with different arguments, looks like a reasonable next step. Forty times in a row.

I'd still pull the actual transcript to confirm rather than assume, specifically looking at whether the agent ever seems to consider stopping, or whether the loop structure is just 'call something, check if satisfied, if not call something else' with no explicit exit condition besides success or hitting the outer timeout. If there's no iteration cap and no instruction anywhere telling it when to give up and escalate, that architecture alone guarantees this failure mode will keep happening whenever the agent is even slightly unsure, tool ambiguity or not.

So I'd fix this in layers rather than one patch. The most direct fix, since this regression tracks exactly with adding the second tool, is tightening both tools' descriptions so it's unambiguous which one applies to which situation -- that alone probably kills most of this 5%. But I wouldn't stop there, because the next ambiguous tool we add will cause the same thing again if the only safety net is good tool descriptions. I'd add a hard cap on tool calls per task, set well under the timeout, so a confused agent fails fast and loud instead of burning 40 calls silently. And I'd add an explicit step after a handful of failed attempts that forces a decision: try something meaningfully different, hand back a partial answer, or flag it for a human -- anything other than quietly trying another near-identical variation.

questions.title: An Agent Took a Destructive Action That Should Have Needed Approval
questions.prompt: Your internal ops agent is designed so that any action tagged "destructive" (deleting records, canceling subscriptions, issuing refunds over $500) requires explicit human approval before executing. Last week, it autonomously canceled 14 active customer subscriptions without any approval step firing, during a task where it was asked to "clean up duplicate trial subscriptions." The approval middleware exists and works correctly in your test suite. Diagnose how a guardrail that passes tests in isolation failed in production, and describe your fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
A guardrail that passes isolated tests but fails in a real task usually means the guardrail is correctly implemented for the cases it was tested against, but the real failure happened at a boundary the tests didn't cover -- most likely, the cancellation wasn't invoked through the path the middleware actually gates. A common version of this: the approval middleware wraps a specific `cancel_subscription` tool call, and tests confirm that calling that tool triggers approval correctly. But if the agent, in pursuit of 'clean up duplicate trial subscriptions,' found or was given a different path to the same effect -- e.g. a more general `update_subscription_status` tool, or a batch/bulk operation tool that wasn't tagged as destructive even though setting status to canceled is exactly that -- the middleware never saw a call it was configured to intercept, because the tagging is per-tool-name rather than per-effect.

To confirm, I'd pull the actual tool call trace from the incident and check exactly which tool(s) the agent invoked to perform the 14 cancellations, then check whether that specific tool or call pattern is covered by the approval middleware's gating logic -- I'd expect to find either an untagged tool that produces the same destructive effect, or a batch call that bypasses a check written for single-item calls.

The fix needs to close the gap between 'tagged as destructive' and 'has a destructive effect.' Rather than tagging individual tool names, gate on the actual effect/outcome where possible (e.g. any write that sets subscription status to canceled requires approval, regardless of which tool or code path produced it), ideally by moving the check down to the data-layer or API boundary rather than the agent's tool-calling layer, so it can't be routed around by using a different tool. Also audit the full tool surface available to this agent for any other tool that can produce a destructive effect without being tagged, since this is unlikely to be the only gap. Finally, add test cases that specifically try to reach the same destructive outcome via alternate tools/paths, not just the primary one, so the test suite actually covers bypass scenarios rather than only the intended path.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The detail 'the middleware works fine in the test suite' tells me this isn't a bug in the approval logic itself -- it's a coverage gap. Something passed tests because the tests only exercised the path everyone assumed would be used, and in production the agent found a different path to the same destructive outcome that nobody wired the gate onto.

So my first move is to go get the actual tool call trace from that incident and see exactly what got called to cancel those 14 subscriptions. My working theory, before I even look, is that there's more than one way to cancel a subscription in this system -- a dedicated cancel tool that's properly tagged and gated, and probably some more general update or batch tool that can set the same status field but was never tagged as destructive because whoever built the guardrail was thinking tool-by-tool rather than effect-by-effect. If that's what the trace shows, it explains everything: the agent wasn't being clever or malicious, it just picked a reasonable-looking tool for a bulk cleanup task, and that tool happened to sit outside the gate.

The fix I'd push for is moving away from gating specific tool names and toward gating the actual effect -- anything that writes a cancellation to a subscription record should require approval no matter which code path produced that write, which usually means pushing the check down closer to the data layer or the underlying API rather than keeping it purely at the agent's tool-calling layer where it's easy to route around. I'd also use this incident as a reason to audit the rest of this agent's tool surface for the same pattern, because if one destructive action had an ungated alternate path, there's a good chance others do too. And for the test suite specifically, I'd add cases that deliberately try to reach the same destructive outcome through a different tool, since the existing tests clearly only proved the intended path works, not that there's no unintended one.
questions.example: The incident trace shows the agent called a generic batch_update_subscriptions(status="canceled") tool rather than the gated cancel_subscription tool -- the approval middleware was only wired to intercept the latter.
commonMistakes: Assuming the approval middleware has a bug and re-testing it in isolation, when the tests already pass
Blaming the agent's judgment/prompt for 'deciding' to skip approval, when the real issue is an ungated tool path
Fixing it by adding approval only to the specific tool used in this incident, without auditing for other ungated paths to the same effect
Gating at the agent's tool-calling layer only, which remains bypassable by any future tool with the same effect
Not updating the test suite to cover alternate-path bypass scenarios, leaving the same class of gap undetected going forward
keyPoints: Recognize that passing isolated tests but failing in production points to a coverage gap, not a logic bug in the guardrail
Identify that the agent likely reached the destructive effect via an untagged/alternate tool path
Propose pulling the actual tool call trace to confirm which path was used
Propose gating on effect/outcome (e.g. at the data or API layer) rather than per-tool-name tagging
Propose auditing the full tool surface and adding bypass-path test coverage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames this as a coverage gap rather than a bug in the existing guardrail logic
Identifies an untagged/alternate tool path as the likely mechanism
Proposes pulling the actual call trace to confirm the bypass path
Proposes effect-based gating (closer to data/API layer) as the structural fix
Proposes auditing the broader tool surface and adding bypass-path test coverage

questions.title: Model-Serving Container Crashes Only in the Cloud
questions.prompt: A containerized model-serving app runs fine on your local machine (16GB RAM, same Docker image) but repeatedly crashes with an OOM kill a few minutes after startup when deployed to your cloud environment, which is provisioned with 8GB of memory per pod based on your team's typical service sizing. The model weights are roughly 6GB on disk. Logs show memory climbing steadily rather than spiking suddenly. Diagnose the likely cause(s) of the mismatch between local and cloud behavior, and describe your fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
The core issue is almost certainly that the pod's memory limit was set using 'typical service' sizing heuristics rather than ML-specific sizing, and it doesn't leave enough headroom above the model's own footprint. A 6GB on-disk model typically needs meaningfully more than 6GB of RAM once loaded: depending on format and framework, loading can involve holding both a serialized/compressed representation and the deserialized in-memory tensors simultaneously during load, plus framework overhead (runtime, CUDA context if applicable, request buffers, KV-cache or batching buffers that grow with traffic). Locally, 16GB gives enough slack to absorb all of that without issue; at 8GB, the pod may just barely fit the idle model but then OOM as real request traffic adds growing buffers on top -- consistent with memory climbing steadily rather than spiking immediately at startup, which points to a leak-like accumulation under load rather than purely a fixed loading overhead problem.

To confirm, I'd profile actual memory usage inside a pod at the same 8GB limit, both at idle right after model load and under a steady stream of requests, to see whether the climb is proportional to request volume (pointing to per-request buffer accumulation or a leak) or happens even with zero traffic (pointing to loading overhead or lazy initialization that keeps allocating after startup). I'd also diff the actual runtime environment -- CPU-only vs GPU, framework version, batch size defaults -- between local and cloud, since 'same image' doesn't guarantee the same effective resource usage if hardware-dependent code paths differ.

The fix starts with right-sizing the pod's memory limit based on measured peak usage under realistic load, not a generic service-sizing default -- likely needing closer to 12-16GB for a 6GB model with request-time buffers, or a smaller model/quantized weights if that's not feasible. If the steady climb under load indicates an actual leak (e.g. request-scoped tensors or cache entries not being released), that needs to be fixed in the serving code directly, which the local test never surfaced because local traffic volume and duration were both far lower during manual testing. Going forward, load-test any ML-serving container at its intended production memory limit before deploying, rather than relying on a 'runs fine locally' check on a machine with 2x the memory.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The number that jumps out at me first is 8GB of pod memory against roughly 6GB of model weights on disk -- that's a thin margin for an ML workload, and 'typical service sizing' almost never accounts for the fact that a model's in-memory footprint after loading is usually bigger than its on-disk size, sometimes meaningfully so depending on format and framework overhead. Locally we've got 16GB, which just papers over that gap entirely, so 'runs fine locally' doesn't actually tell us the memory profile is healthy -- it tells us we have slack we don't have in the cloud.

The detail I'd weight most heavily, though, is that memory climbs steadily rather than spiking at startup. A pure loading-overhead problem would usually show up as a jump right after the model loads and then flatten out. Steady climb over several minutes smells more like something accumulating with traffic -- request buffers, a cache that's not evicting, KV-cache growth if this is a generative model, something scoped per-request that isn't getting released. So I'd actually profile memory inside a pod capped at 8GB, both right after load with zero traffic and then under a steady request stream, to see which of those two stories -- pure headroom shortage versus an actual per-request leak -- is really going on, because the fix is different depending on which it is.

If it's pure headroom, the fix is just right-sizing the pod to what the model and its runtime actually need under real load, not what a generic service-sizing rule of thumb says -- probably somewhere north of 12GB for a 6GB model with buffers, confirmed by the load test rather than guessed. If it's a genuine leak, that's a code fix in the serving layer, and the reason local testing never caught it is that nobody ran it long enough or with enough concurrent traffic locally for a slow leak to become visible before someone closed the test and moved on. Either way, I'd make load-testing at the actual production memory limit a standard step before any ML-serving deploy, because 'it ran on my 16GB laptop for five minutes' was never going to catch this.
questions.code:
$ kubectl top pod model-server-7f9c -n prod
NAME              CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
model-server-7f9c   410m         7918Mi   # climbing from ~6.1Gi at t+0 to OOM at t+4min
questions.example: Load-testing the same image inside an 8GB-capped local container (using docker run --memory=8g) and sending a sustained stream of requests reproduces the same steady climb to OOM within a few minutes, confirming the issue is reproducible outside the cloud once memory is actually constrained to match.
commonMistakes: Assuming the cloud environment itself is misconfigured (networking, storage) rather than checking memory limits against actual usage
Treating 'runs fine locally' as proof the app is memory-healthy, without accounting for the 16GB vs 8GB headroom difference
Fixing it by simply bumping the memory limit without first checking whether the steady climb indicates an actual leak under load
Not reproducing the issue in a memory-constrained local container, relying only on cloud logs for diagnosis
Overlooking framework/runtime overhead (buffers, caches, request-scoped state) as part of the model's real memory footprint beyond its on-disk size
keyPoints: Recognize that on-disk model size understates actual in-memory footprint once loaded with framework overhead
Identify the local-vs-cloud memory headroom difference (16GB vs 8GB) as masking the issue locally
Distinguish steady-climb-under-load (leak/accumulation) from startup-spike (pure loading overhead) based on the log pattern
Propose profiling memory inside a pod at the actual production limit, both idle and under load
Propose right-sizing the memory limit based on measured peak usage and/or fixing an underlying leak if confirmed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies insufficient memory headroom relative to model size and framework overhead as a key factor
Explains why local (16GB) masks the issue that surfaces at cloud's 8GB limit
Correctly interprets the steady-climb pattern as pointing to load-driven accumulation, not just startup overhead
Proposes concrete profiling at the actual production memory limit under load
Proposes a correct fix path (right-sizing and/or fixing a leak) based on profiling results

questions.title: p99 Latency Dominated by Cold Starts After a New Autoscaling Policy
questions.prompt: After rolling out a new autoscaling policy meant to cut idle infrastructure cost for your AI inference service, p50 latency is unchanged at 180ms, but p99 latency jumped from 400ms to 6.5 seconds. The new policy scales pods down to zero replicas after 5 minutes of no traffic, versus the previous policy's minimum of 2 always-on replicas. Traffic is bursty: steady for stretches, then idle for 10-20 minutes, then a burst of requests. Diagnose why p99 degraded so sharply while p50 stayed flat, and describe your fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
The p50/p99 split is the whole diagnosis: p50 stays flat because most requests arrive while at least one replica is already warm and serving steadily, so the typical request's experience is unchanged. p99 exploded because the new policy introduces a scale-to-zero cold start specifically for the first request(s) after any idle gap longer than 5 minutes -- and the traffic pattern described (steady, then 10-20 minute idle stretches, then bursts) means this exact scenario recurs repeatedly throughout the day. A cold start for an AI inference service is often dominated by model load time (pulling the container image if not cached, initializing the runtime, loading potentially multi-gigabyte model weights into memory or GPU), which easily accounts for several seconds, landing squarely in the tail that p99 measures. Because it's specifically the first request(s) after each idle gap that pay this cost, and the traffic pattern guarantees multiple such gaps per day, a meaningful fraction of requests fall into the worst percentile.

To confirm, I'd correlate the timestamp of each slow (>1s) request with how long the service had been idle beforehand and whether a scale-up event occurred in the preceding seconds -- I'd expect a near-perfect correlation between 'this request triggered or immediately followed a cold start' and 'this request is in the p99 tail.' I'd also directly measure cold start duration in isolation (time from scale-up trigger to ready-to-serve) to confirm it's in the multi-second range matching the observed p99.

The fix needs to preserve most of the cost savings while eliminating the worst-case latency. Options, often combined: keep a small minimum replica count (e.g. 1 instead of 0) rather than true scale-to-zero, which cuts idle cost significantly versus the old policy's 2-replica minimum while avoiding cold starts entirely; if scale-to-zero is kept for deeper cost savings during long idle periods, add a warm-pool or pre-warming mechanism that scales up proactively based on a leading indicator (e.g. a lightweight health-check/traffic-prediction trigger) rather than reactively after the first request already arrived; and separately, reduce the cold start's own duration -- smaller/optimized container images, lazy vs eager model loading tuned appropriately, and keeping model weights in a fast, already-warm cache rather than re-pulling them from cold storage on every scale-up.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The fact that p50 didn't move at all but p99 went from 400ms to 6.5 seconds tells me this isn't a general performance regression -- it's isolated to a specific subset of requests, and given what changed, that subset is obviously 'the first request after the service scaled down to zero.' Most traffic still hits an already-warm replica, which is why the median is untouched; it's only the unlucky requests that happen to land right after one of those 10-20 minute idle gaps that are eating the cold start cost, and given the bursty traffic pattern described, that's going to happen multiple times a day, every day.

I'd want to confirm that correlation directly rather than just assume it, so I'd pull timestamps for the slow requests and check how long the service had been idle right before each one, and whether a scale-up event fired in the seconds leading up to it. I'd bet that's a near-perfect match. And for an AI inference service specifically, I'm not surprised a cold start lands in the multiple-seconds range -- pulling a container image if it's not cached, spinning up the runtime, and loading model weights that could be gigabytes in size, that's genuinely slow work, and it's exactly the kind of cost that scale-to-zero policies tend to ignore because they're usually designed with lightweight stateless services in mind, not model-serving workloads.

Given the traffic pattern is bursty with real idle gaps, I don't think true scale-to-zero was ever the right call for cost savings here, and I'd propose keeping at least one warm replica at all times instead of zero -- that alone probably recovers most of the p99 regression while still cutting cost meaningfully versus the old two-replica minimum. If there's a strong reason to still want deeper savings during the longest idle stretches, I'd look at a pre-warming approach instead of pure reactive scaling -- something that starts spinning up a replica slightly ahead of an expected burst rather than only after the first request has already arrived and is waiting. And separately from the policy itself, I'd want to shrink the cold start duration on its own merits -- trimming the container image, making sure model weights are loaded from a fast warm cache rather than cold storage -- since that benefit applies no matter what scaling policy we land on.
questions.example: Setting the minimum replica count to 1 instead of 0 while keeping the rest of the autoscaling policy unchanged dropped p99 latency back to roughly 420ms in a side-by-side test, while idle infra cost still fell significantly versus the old 2-replica minimum.
commonMistakes: Investigating general service performance (code, database, network) instead of correlating slow requests with idle-gap and scale-up events
Treating p50 being unaffected as evidence the new policy is fine overall, without examining what specifically drives the tail
Fixing it by increasing timeout/retry settings on the client side instead of addressing the cold start itself
Reverting the entire autoscaling policy back to 2 always-on replicas, giving up all cost savings instead of finding a middle ground (e.g. min 1 replica, pre-warming)
Not measuring actual cold start duration in isolation, leaving the root cause as an assumption rather than a confirmed number
keyPoints: Correctly reason that an unaffected p50 with a spiked p99 means the issue is isolated to a specific request subset, not a general regression
Identify scale-to-zero cold starts after idle gaps as that subset, matching the described bursty traffic pattern
Explain why AI inference cold starts (image pull, runtime init, model weight loading) are especially slow
Propose a confirmation method correlating slow requests with idle duration and scale-up timestamps
Propose a fix that balances cost savings and latency (minimum warm replica, pre-warming, and/or reducing cold start duration itself)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons from the p50/p99 split to an isolated-subset cause
Identifies scale-to-zero cold starts correlated with idle gaps as the root cause
Explains why AI model-serving cold starts are especially costly in time
Proposes a concrete confirmation method
Proposes a balanced fix (min warm replica and/or pre-warming and/or reduced cold start duration)

questions.title: Multi-Model Routing Across Chat, Summarization, and Reasoning Features
questions.prompt: Your product has three LLM-powered features: a real-time chat assistant needing sub-1-second first-token latency at 2M requests/day, an overnight batch summarization job processing 500K documents that just needs to finish inside an 8-hour window, and a complex financial-reasoning feature used by a small number of power users where accuracy matters far more than cost or speed. A teammate proposes standardizing on one frontier model everywhere to 'keep things simple.' Design the model-selection and routing architecture you'd actually build, and justify when a single model is the right call versus when multi-model routing earns its complexity.
questions.modelAnswer:
A single model forces every feature onto the same point of the cost-latency-quality frontier, and that point can't be optimal for all three simultaneously. Chat needs a small, fast model because latency is the binding constraint and the task doesn't require frontier-level reasoning. Batch summarization is throughput-bound, not latency-bound, so it should use whichever model has the best cost-per-token at scale, potentially via an async batch API that trades turnaround time for a meaningful discount. The reasoning feature is accuracy-bound with low volume, so paying for the frontier model with a larger token budget is the correct trade because the cost per request is immaterial against the value of a correct answer.

The architecture is a routing layer behind a single internal API so application code never hardcodes a provider or model name. Routing should be done by feature identity, not by inspecting request content, because the three features are already known at the call site — this avoids latency and a new failure mode in the hot path. Each route carries its own config: model, timeout, retry policy, fallback model, and prompt-template version. The gateway centralizes logging of tokens, latency, and cost per route so degradation in any one feature is visible independently, and gives you one place to add a cheaper fallback model if the primary model's cost or availability changes.

Multi-model routing earns its complexity once you have evidence a feature is being over- or under-served — extra eval suites, provider contracts, and prompt-drift management per model are ongoing costs. For an early-stage product, low volume, or a small team, a single capable model is the right default; you split only when a specific feature's SLA is measurably violated and the fix can't be achieved by tuning prompts or parameters on the one model you already run.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by pushing back on 'simplicity' as the only axis and put the numbers on the board: chat needs sub-second time-to-first-token at 2M/day, so I need something small and cheap per call; summarization has a loose latency budget but huge volume, so I care about dollars per token at scale; reasoning has almost no volume but a high bar for correctness, so I'd happily pay far more per call if it meaningfully reduces wrong answers for power users making real decisions off it.

From there I'd sketch a gateway: all three features call one internal endpoint, the gateway looks at which feature is calling — not the content of the request — and routes to a model config for that feature: a small fast model for chat, a batch-discounted model for the overnight job, and the frontier model with a bigger budget for reasoning. I'd keep prompt templates and model names out of application code entirely so swapping providers later is a config change, not a redeploy, and I'd log cost, latency, and token counts per route from day one so I can show, with data, whether a route is mis-served rather than guessing.

The honest caveat I'd give the teammate is that I wouldn't build all three routes on day one for a new product — I'd ship on one solid model and only fork a route once I have a concrete SLA violation to point to, because every extra model is another eval suite, another vendor relationship, and another thing that can silently drift. Multi-model routing is a scaling response to proven pain, not a starting posture.
questions.example: Gateway config sketch: chat -> small fast model, 2s timeout, same-tier fallback provider; summarization -> batch API endpoint, 24h SLA, no fallback needed; reasoning -> frontier model, extended token budget, human-review flag on low-confidence output. All three share one prompt-versioning and logging layer.
commonMistakes: Choosing the model per request by running a classifier on content instead of routing by the already-known feature identity, adding latency and a new failure mode
Hardcoding model names and prompt templates directly in each feature's code instead of behind a shared gateway, making future swaps a multi-file change
Building all three routes speculatively before any feature has shown a measurable SLA violation
Ignoring that batch APIs offer meaningful cost discounts for the summarization job's loose latency budget
Not tracking per-route cost, latency, and accuracy separately, so a degrading feature is invisible until users complain
keyPoints: Each feature sits at a different point on the cost-latency-quality frontier; no single model is optimal for all three
Route by feature identity at the call site, not by classifying request content in the hot path
Centralize model config, prompt versions, and fallback behavior behind one internal gateway abstraction
Batch-oriented features should exploit asynchronous batch pricing rather than paying for real-time latency they don't need
Multi-model complexity should be adopted reactively, justified by measured SLA violations, not adopted speculatively

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly maps each feature's constraints to a distinct point on the cost/latency/quality frontier
Proposes a coherent gateway/routing architecture decoupled from application code
Identifies batch pricing or throughput-oriented handling for the summarization workload
Articulates clear criteria for when a single model is sufficient vs. when routing pays off
Addresses observability/monitoring per route

questions.title: Choosing Between Fine-Tuning, RAG, and Prompting for Ticket Triage
questions.prompt: A company wants an internal assistant that triages support tickets into categories and routes them, using company-specific product names, internal jargon, and historical resolution patterns a general-purpose model doesn't know. They have 50,000 historical labeled tickets and a knowledge base of 2,000 internal articles that changes weekly. Design the decision framework for choosing between prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning (or some combination), and specify which signals in this scenario push you toward each option.
questions.modelAnswer:
The three techniques solve different problems: prompting injects instructions and examples at inference time, RAG injects current factual knowledge at inference time, and fine-tuning bakes a behavior or style into model weights permanently. The decision framework should separate 'what does the model need to know' from 'how should the model behave,' because triage has both a knowledge component (the 2,000-article KB, which changes weekly) and a behavior component (consistent categorization into the company's taxonomy).

The weekly-changing KB is the strongest signal for RAG over fine-tuning: retraining weekly is operationally expensive and the model would still hallucinate on content added after the last training cut. RAG retrieves the current article at query time, so freshness is solved structurally. The 50,000 labeled tickets are a strong signal for fine-tuning if the taxonomy and the ticket-to-category pattern is stable, because a fine-tuned classifier will be far cheaper and more consistent at inference than stuffing hundreds of examples into every prompt via few-shot. If the taxonomy itself shifts frequently, prompting with a small curated example set is more maintainable than retraining.

In practice the right system combines them: a fine-tuned or few-shot classifier handles category and routing using patterns learned from the 50K tickets, while a RAG layer retrieves the most relevant article(s) to ground any suggested-resolution text shown to the agent. Pure prompting alone is insufficient because jargon and historical patterns exceed what fits reliably in a context window across thousands of daily tickets, and pure fine-tuning alone is insufficient because it can't keep the KB current without constant retraining.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd separate this into two questions before picking a technique: what does the assistant need to know, and what does it need to do consistently. Jargon and historical patterns sound like 'knowledge,' but routing into a fixed taxonomy is a behavior/consistency problem — those pull toward different solutions, and conflating them is how teams end up fine-tuning when they should have built a retrieval layer, or the reverse.

The KB changing weekly is the detail that settles it for me: anything that goes stale on a weekly cycle is a bad fit for fine-tuning, because I'd be retraining constantly and still serving stale answers in the gap — that's a RAG problem, so I'd index the 2,000 articles and retrieve the top few per ticket. The 50K labeled tickets are a different story: if the taxonomy is stable, that's exactly the kind of large, consistent labeled dataset fine-tuning is good at, and it'll be cheaper and more consistent at inference than cramming representative examples into every prompt.

So the system I'd actually build is a fine-tuned classifier for category and routing, sitting in front of a RAG layer that pulls the current article to ground any suggested resolution. I'd avoid pure prompting here because jargon-heavy few-shot examples bloat every single call's token cost across a high-volume ticket stream, and I'd treat the taxonomy's stability as the trigger for revisiting the fine-tune — if categories start shifting monthly, I'd switch that piece back to prompting instead.
questions.example: Pipeline: incoming ticket -> fine-tuned classifier assigns category + routing queue -> RAG layer retrieves top 3 relevant KB articles for that category -> suggested-resolution draft composed from retrieved content, shown to a human agent for approval.
commonMistakes: Fine-tuning on the weekly-changing knowledge base instead of the stable labeled-ticket patterns, causing constant costly retraining
Treating jargon/knowledge and categorization/behavior as the same problem and applying one technique to both
Relying on pure few-shot prompting with company jargon baked into every prompt, bloating token cost and context budget
Skipping a retrieval evaluation step, so stale or irrelevant articles get retrieved and silently degrade triage quality
Fine-tuning a full generative model for classification instead of considering a smaller, cheaper fine-tuned classifier or constrained output
keyPoints: Separate 'what the model needs to know' (knowledge, favors RAG) from 'how it should behave' (consistency/taxonomy, favors fine-tuning)
A weekly-changing knowledge base is a strong signal against fine-tuning and for RAG due to staleness
A large, stable labeled dataset with a fixed taxonomy is a strong signal for fine-tuning a classifier
Pure prompting fails at scale when jargon and context exceed a maintainable context window across high ticket volume
The strongest real-world design combines techniques rather than picking one exclusively

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the decision around knowledge-freshness vs. behavior-consistency
Uses the weekly-changing KB as the deciding signal for RAG over fine-tuning
Uses the 50K labeled tickets as the deciding signal for fine-tuning a classifier
Proposes a combined architecture rather than an exclusive single-technique answer
Notes operational cost/maintenance tradeoffs of each option

questions.title: Handling a 90-Day Model Deprecation Across Dozens of Dependent Prompts
questions.prompt: A provider announces a 90-day deprecation window for the model your product has standardized on. Dozens of prompts across a dozen features depend on that model's specific behavior — some rely on its exact formatting quirks, some on tone, some on reasoning style. Design the system and process you'd put in place so this deprecation (and the next one) doesn't become a fire drill, including how you'd validate the replacement model before cutting traffic over.
questions.modelAnswer:
The root problem is that prompts were allowed to become implicitly coupled to a specific model's quirks rather than to a documented, testable contract. The fix starts with an eval set per feature — a set of representative inputs with expected properties (format, tone constraints, factual correctness) captured before migration begins. Without this, you have no objective way to know whether the new model broke a feature or just behaves differently in a way nobody actually depends on.

The migration itself should run as a parallel shadow deployment: route a copy of live traffic (or the eval set, at minimum) to the candidate model, diff outputs against the current model's outputs and against the eval set's expected properties, and quantify regression per feature rather than per the whole product. Features should be migrated in order of eval confidence and business risk — low-risk, well-covered features first, to validate the migration tooling itself before touching the riskiest prompts. Any prompt that was implicitly depending on formatting quirks (e.g. exact whitespace, a specific refusal phrasing) needs its downstream parsing hardened or its prompt made explicit about the required format, since that fragility was latent before the deprecation ever forced it to the surface.

For the next deprecation to not be a fire drill, the system should track model dependency per prompt in a central registry, run the eval suite automatically against new model versions on a schedule (not only when forced), and keep the routing/gateway abstraction from the model-selection design so switching the underlying model is a config change validated by the eval suite, not a code change discovered under a deadline.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move isn't picking a replacement model — it's admitting that the real problem is we never had a contract for what these prompts actually depend on, only a de facto one based on what this specific model happened to output. So step one is building or dusting off an eval set per feature: real inputs, with assertions about what a correct response looks like, independent of model-specific phrasing.

Then I'd treat the migration like any other risky deployment — shadow traffic to the candidate model, diff against current outputs and against the eval assertions, and look feature by feature rather than asking 'does the new model seem fine' in the aggregate. I'd deliberately migrate the lowest-risk, best-covered features first, partly to validate my own migration tooling before I bet anything important on it. Anywhere a prompt turns out to be silently relying on an exact formatting quirk, I'd treat that as a bug I'm glad got surfaced, not just a casualty of the deprecation, and fix the downstream parsing or make the format explicit in the prompt.

Longer term, the fix is structural: a registry of which model each prompt depends on, an eval suite that runs against new model versions automatically and continuously rather than only when a deprecation notice forces it, and the same model-routing abstraction I'd want anyway so a model swap is a config change behind a gateway, validated by evals, instead of a scramble through a dozen codebases in a 90-day window.
questions.example: Migration order: Phase 1 — features with existing eval coverage and low business risk (shadow traffic, diff, cut over). Phase 2 — medium-risk features, harden any parsing found to depend on old-model formatting quirks. Phase 3 — highest-risk reasoning-heavy features, migrated last with manual review of a sample before full cutover.
commonMistakes: Having no eval set captured before migration, so regressions are only caught by users after cutover
Migrating all features simultaneously instead of in risk-ordered phases
Assuming aggregate 'looks similar' output quality means every individual feature is unaffected
Not auditing for implicit dependencies on the old model's exact formatting or refusal phrasing before cutover
Treating this deprecation as a one-off fire drill instead of building a registry and recurring eval process for the next one
keyPoints: Prompts were implicitly coupled to model-specific quirks rather than a documented, testable contract
Build or reuse a per-feature eval set with explicit expected properties before migrating
Use shadow traffic and output diffing to quantify regression per feature, not product-wide
Migrate in risk-ordered phases, validating migration tooling on low-risk features first
Fix the systemic gap afterward: a model-dependency registry and continuous eval runs against new model versions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the root cause as implicit coupling to model-specific behavior rather than a documented contract
Proposes a concrete pre-migration eval set with explicit expected properties
